section_html:
Temperament

Temperament refers to individual differences in emotional reactivity and self-regulation that appear early in life, show moderate stability over time, and are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. The most influential classification was developed by Thomas and Chess (1977) based on the New York Longitudinal Study (NYLS).

Thomas and Chess's Three Temperament Types

Easy child (~40%): Positive mood, regular biological rhythms, adaptable, moderate intensity of reaction.
Difficult child (~10%): Negative mood, irregular rhythms, slow to adapt, intense reactions.
Slow-to-warm-up child (~15%): Initially negative, low activity level, slow adaptation, mildly intense reactions. The remaining ~35% showed mixed patterns.

Thomas and Chess introduced the concept of goodness of fit—the match between a child's temperament and the demands and expectations of the caregiving environment. A difficult child in a patient, flexible environment may thrive, while the same child in a rigid, punitive environment may develop behavioral problems.

Exam Example

A parent describes their 6-month-old as fussy, with unpredictable eating and sleeping schedules, and strong emotional reactions to new situations. Using Thomas and Chess's classification, this infant would be described as having a "difficult" temperament. A clinician would focus on goodness of fit between the child's temperament and parenting approach.

Kagan's Behavioral Inhibition

Jerome Kagan identified a temperamental dimension called behavioral inhibition—the tendency to react with wariness and withdrawal to novel or unfamiliar stimuli. Approximately 15–20% of infants are classified as behaviorally inhibited. Kagan's longitudinal research showed that inhibited infants tend to remain cautious and shy into childhood, and they show a heightened risk for developing anxiety disorders, particularly social anxiety.

Thomas, A., & Chess, S. (1977). Temperament and development. Brunner/Mazel.
prev_last_paragraph: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of attachment. Erlbaum.

section_html:
Conduct Disorder (CD)

Conduct Disorder involves a repetitive and persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms are violated. The DSM-5 requires at least 3 of 15 criteria in the past 12 months, with at least 1 criterion present in the past 6 months, across four categories:

Symptom Categories

CategoryExamples
Aggression to people and animalsBullying, initiating fights, using weapons, physical cruelty to people or animals, forcing sexual activity
Destruction of propertyDeliberately setting fires, deliberately destroying property
Deceitfulness or theftBreaking into someone's house/car, lying to obtain goods, shoplifting
Serious violations of rulesStaying out late (before age 13), running away, truancy (before age 13)

Onset Specifiers

Childhood-Onset vs. Adolescent-Onset

Childhood-onset type: At least one criterion characteristic of CD prior to age 10. Associated with more persistent aggression, worse prognosis, and higher likelihood of developing ASPD in adulthood. Adolescent-onset type: No criteria present prior to age 10. Associated with less aggression, more influence of deviant peers, and a better prognosis. Unspecified onset: Criteria met but insufficient information to determine onset.

The Callous-Unemotional (CU) Specifier

The DSM-5 added the specifier "with limited prosocial emotions" (the callous-unemotional traits specifier). To qualify, the individual must display at least two of the following persistently over at least 12 months and in multiple settings:

  • Lack of remorse or guilt -- does not feel bad about misbehavior
  • Callous -- lack of empathy -- disregards others' feelings
  • Unconcerned about performance -- does not show concern about poor performance at school, work, or other activities
  • Shallow or deficient affect -- does not express emotions or appears insincere

EPPP Example

Children with CD and CU traits show distinct neurobiological features: reduced amygdala reactivity to fearful facial expressions, lower cortisol reactivity to stress, and diminished autonomic arousal (Frick et al., 2014). They tend to show proactive (instrumental) aggression rather than reactive aggression, and they respond poorly to punishment-based interventions but may respond to reward-based approaches.
prev_last_paragraph: ODD prevalence is approximately 3.3%, with a male predominance in childhood that equalizes by adolescence. It typically emerges in the preschool years and is usually evident before age 8. ODD often precedes the development of conduct disorder, but the majority of children with ODD do not progress to conduct disorder.

section_html:
Anorexia Nervosa (AN)

Anorexia nervosa is characterized by restriction of energy intake leading to a significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight, and disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced.

DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria

  1. Criterion A: Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health
  2. Criterion B: Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though at a significantly low weight
  3. Criterion C: Disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body weight/shape on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight

Subtypes

  • Restricting type: Weight loss achieved primarily through dieting, fasting, and/or excessive exercise. No recurrent binge-eating or purging in the past 3 months.
  • Binge-eating/purging type: Recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging (self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas) during the past 3 months.

Clinical Pearl

DSM-5 made several important changes to AN criteria: (1) removed the specific BMI threshold and the word "refusal" to eat, replacing it with "restriction"; (2) removed the amenorrhea criterion, recognizing that AN occurs in males and post-menopausal women; (3) Criterion B no longer requires explicit acknowledgment of fear of weight gain -- persistent behavior interfering with weight gain suffices.

Medical Complications

AN has the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric disorder, approximately 5-10% per decade of illness. Deaths result from medical complications (cardiac arrhythmias, electrolyte imbalances) and suicide. Key medical findings include bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo hair, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome (dangerous electrolyte shifts upon nutritional restoration, particularly hypophosphatemia).
prev_heading_text: Overview of Feeding and Eating Disorders
prev_last_paragraph: Fairburn's (2003) transdiagnostic model proposes that eating disorders share a core psychopathology: the over-evaluation of eating, shape, and weight, and their control. This model is the basis for enhanced cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT-E), which can be applied across eating disorder diagnoses.

section_html:
Cluster C: Anxious or Fearful

Cluster C personality disorders are characterized by anxious and fearful behavior. They share features with anxiety disorders but are distinguished by their pervasiveness and ego-syntonic quality.

Avoidant Personality Disorder

A pervasive pattern of social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation. Features include avoidance of occupational activities involving interpersonal contact due to fear of criticism, unwillingness to get involved unless certain of being liked, restraint in intimate relationships due to shame, preoccupation with rejection in social situations, inhibited in new interpersonal situations, views self as inept/unappealing/inferior, and reluctance to take personal risks or engage in new activities.

Avoidant PD and social anxiety disorder share significant overlap. The key distinction is that avoidant PD involves a more pervasive pattern of avoidance and a more deeply ingrained sense of personal inadequacy that extends beyond specific social performance situations (Lampe & Malhi, 2018).

Dependent Personality Disorder

A pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of that leads to submissive and clinging behavior and fears of separation. Features include difficulty making everyday decisions without advice, needing others to assume responsibility for major life areas, difficulty expressing disagreement, difficulty initiating projects independently, going to excessive lengths to obtain nurturance, feeling uncomfortable or helpless when alone, urgently seeking another relationship when one ends, and unrealistic preoccupation with fears of being left to care for oneself.

Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)

A pervasive pattern of preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, and mental and interpersonal control, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and efficiency. Features include preoccupation with details/rules/order, perfectionism interfering with task completion, excessive devotion to work, over-conscientiousness about morality, inability to discard worn-out objects, reluctance to delegate, miserly spending style, and rigidity/stubbornness.

OCPD vs. OCD

OCPD involves ego-syntonic traits -- the person's perfectionism and control feel consistent with who they are. OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions and compulsions -- the person recognizes them as excessive and distressing. OCPD does not involve true obsessions or compulsions. Despite the name similarity, only about 23-32% of individuals with OCD also have OCPD. OCPD is the most prevalent personality disorder in the general population (approximately 3-8%).

prev_last_paragraph: Kohut's self psychology conceptualizes narcissistic pathology as resulting from empathic failures by early caregivers (selfobjects), leading to a fragmented self. Treatment involves providing empathic mirroring and idealizing transferences. Kernberg, in contrast, views narcissistic personality as a pathological grandiose self that defends against underlying aggression and envy, requiring confrontation of defenses in treatment.
