section_html:
Self-Disclosure and Relationship Development

The development of close relationships involves a process of escalating self-disclosure -- the voluntary sharing of personal information that the other person would not otherwise know.

Social Penetration Theory (Altman & Taylor, 1973)

This theory describes relationship development as a process of increasing breadth (range of topics discussed) and depth (level of intimacy of disclosures). Early interactions involve broad but shallow disclosures. As trust develops, disclosures become deeper and more personal. Relationship deterioration involves a reversal of this process -- "depenetration."

Reciprocity of Disclosure

Self-disclosure follows a norm of reciprocity, particularly in early relationship stages. When one person discloses personal information, the other tends to match the level of disclosure. This reciprocal escalation builds trust and intimacy progressively. In therapy, appropriate therapist self-disclosure can model vulnerability and strengthen the therapeutic alliance, though it must be used judiciously and in the client's interest.

Clinical Note on Disclosure

Jourard's (1971) research showed that therapist self-disclosure tends to increase client self-disclosure. However, cultural factors significantly moderate the appropriateness and impact of disclosure. Clients from cultures that value emotional restraint may find therapist self-disclosure inappropriate or confusing, while clients from cultures that value relational warmth may view it as a sign of genuine caring and trust.

Loneliness and Social Isolation

Loneliness is the subjective experience of perceived social isolation -- a discrepancy between desired and actual social connections. It is distinct from objective social isolation (physically being alone). Research shows that loneliness is associated with increased risk for depression, cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline, and mortality. Cacioppo's (2009) evolutionary model of loneliness proposes that loneliness functions as a biological signal (analogous to hunger or thirst) that motivates reconnection with others. However, chronic loneliness creates a self-reinforcing cycle: lonely individuals become hypervigilant to social threats, interpret ambiguous social cues negatively, and withdraw further from social contact.

Weiss's Types of Loneliness (1973)

Robert Weiss distinguished between social loneliness (absence of a social network or sense of community belonging) and emotional loneliness (absence of a close, intimate attachment figure). Different interventions are needed for each type: social loneliness responds to group-based interventions and community integration, while emotional loneliness requires the development of close, confiding relationships. This distinction is clinically important because a person can experience one type without the other.

Interventions for loneliness are most effective when they address maladaptive social cognition (the negative interpretive biases that perpetuate loneliness) rather than simply providing social opportunities. Cognitive-behavioral approaches that target distorted social perceptions have shown the largest effect sizes in meta-analyses (Masi et al., 2011).

Cacioppo, J. T., & Patrick, W. (2008). Loneliness: Human nature and the need for social connection. W. W. Norton.
prev_heading_text: Evolutionary and Sociocultural Perspectives on Mate Selection
prev_last_paragraph: Attraction and relationships questions on the EPPP draw from multiple theoretical perspectives. Be prepared to identify: the four major determinants of attraction, distinguish between Sternberg's seven types of love, map attachment styles onto the two-dimensional model, recognize Gottman's four predictive communication patterns, and understand the theoretical debate between evolutionary and sociocultural explanations for mate preferences. Clinically, attachment theory is the most directly applied framework in therapeutic practice, particularly in Emotionally Focused Therapy.

section_html:
Deindividuation

Definition

Deindividuation is a psychological state of reduced self-awareness and diminished sense of personal identity that can occur in group settings, particularly when individuals feel anonymous. In this state, people are more likely to engage in impulsive, antisocial, or norm-violating behavior because the normal restraints of self-monitoring and concern about evaluation are weakened.

Conditions That Promote Deindividuation

  • Anonymity: Wearing uniforms, masks, or being in darkness reduces identifiability.
  • Large group size: Being one of many reduces the feeling of individual accountability.
  • Arousal: High emotional arousal shifts attention away from self-regulation.
  • Reduced self-awareness: Conditions that focus attention outward (rather than inward) promote deindividuation.

Key Research

Zimbardo (1969) demonstrated that participants wearing hoods and lab coats (anonymous condition) delivered more intense shocks than identifiable participants. Diener et al. (1976) found that trick-or-treating children in costumes (anonymous) stole more candy when in groups than when alone or identifiable.

Clinical and Practical Relevance

Deindividuation helps explain mob behavior, online trolling and cyberbullying (where anonymity is high), and the behavior of individuals in institutional settings (e.g., the Stanford Prison Experiment). Understanding deindividuation is relevant to workplace consultation, school psychology, and forensic evaluations. Interventions that increase self-awareness and accountability (mirrors, cameras, name tags) can counteract deindividuation effects.

Summary Table: Group Influence Phenomena

PhenomenonKey Researcher(s)Core Finding
ConformityAsch; SherifPeople change behavior to match group norms
ObedienceMilgram65% obeyed authority to maximum shock level
Social facilitationZajoncOthers enhance dominant responses
Social loafingLatane et al.Less effort in groups when individual effort is not identifiable
GroupthinkJanisCohesive groups make defective decisions
Group polarizationMoscovici & ZavalloniDiscussion intensifies initial group tendency
DeindividuationZimbardoAnonymity in groups reduces self-regulation
Zimbardo, P. G. (2007). The Lucifer effect: Understanding how good people turn evil. Random House.
prev_last_paragraph: Group polarization is distinct from groupthink. Group polarization describes the direction of the shift (toward the extreme of the initial tendency), while groupthink describes a process of defective decision-making in cohesive groups. A group can polarize without experiencing groupthink, and groupthink involves more than just polarization.

section_html:
The Bystander Effect

The bystander effect refers to the finding that individuals are less likely to help in an emergency when other bystanders are present. This phenomenon was studied extensively by Latane and Darley following the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York City.

Latane and Darley's Decision Model of Helping

Latane and Darley (1970) proposed a five-step sequential model. Failure at any step results in no helping:

  1. Notice the event: The bystander must first perceive that something is happening.
  2. Interpret as emergency: The bystander must interpret the situation as one requiring help. Pluralistic ignorance -- looking to others for cues and misinterpreting their inaction as evidence that no emergency exists -- can block this step.
  3. Assume responsibility: The bystander must feel personally responsible for helping. Diffusion of responsibility -- the assumption that someone else will help -- reduces the sense of personal obligation as the number of bystanders increases.
  4. Know how to help: The bystander must have the knowledge or skills to provide assistance.
  5. Decide to help: The bystander must weigh the costs and benefits of intervening and decide to act.

Key Experiment: Seizure Study (Darley & Latane, 1968)

Participants in discussion groups via intercom heard a confederate apparently having a seizure. When participants believed they were the only one who could hear the emergency, 85% helped. When they believed four others were also listening, only 31% helped. This demonstrated diffusion of responsibility directly -- more bystanders led to less individual helping.

While diffusion of responsibility is best known for its role in bystander situations, it is also the construct most useful for explaining social loafing — the phenomenon in which individuals reduce their effort when working collectively on a task. In group work settings, each member may assume that others are contributing sufficiently, leading to a diminished sense of personal accountability. Because responsibility for the group's output feels shared among all members, no single individual feels compelled to exert maximum effort. This parallels the bystander dynamic: just as the presence of multiple witnesses dilutes the felt obligation to intervene, the presence of multiple contributors dilutes the felt obligation to work hard. Strategies that counteract social loafing — such as making individual contributions identifiable or assigning specific roles — work precisely because they restore personal responsibility and eliminate the diffusion effect.

Factors That Increase Helping

  • Clarity of emergency: Unambiguous emergencies produce more helping.
  • Perceived similarity: People help more when the victim is perceived as similar to themselves.
  • Being alone: Lone bystanders help more than those in groups.
  • Feeling competent: People with relevant skills (e.g., medical training) help more.
  • Good mood: Positive mood states increase helping (Isen & Levin, 1972).
  • Rural vs. urban: Helping rates tend to be higher in rural settings, possibly due to less stimulus overload.
Latane, B., & Darley, J. M. (1970). The unresponsive bystander: Why doesn't he help? Appleton-Century-Crofts.
prev_last_paragraph: Empirical research supports the idea that genuinely altruistic motivations have distinct behavioral consequences compared with egoistic ones. In a study examining charitable responses following the September 11, 2001 attacks, Piferi, Jobe, and Jones found that donors reported a range of motivations for giving money and providing other forms of assistance to victims. These motives included self-focused reasons (e.g., feeling better about oneself, social pressure) as well as other-focused reasons centered on improving victims' well-being. Critically, the altruistic motivation — the desire to genuinely enhance the welfare of those affected — was the strongest predictor of continued donations and sustained helping over time. This finding is consistent with Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis: when helping is driven by authentic concern for others rather than by self-oriented benefits, it tends to be more durable and less contingent on situational incentives or emotional relief.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take — How the Mind Judges People
section_html:
Attribution Theory

Attribution is the process by which people explain the causes of behavior and events. The fundamental question in attribution theory is: Did this person behave this way because of who they are (internal/dispositional attribution) or because of the situation they were in (external/situational attribution)?

Fritz Heider: The Father of Attribution Theory

Fritz Heider (1958) introduced the basic distinction between internal (dispositional) attributions — attributing behavior to personal characteristics such as traits, abilities, or effort — and external (situational) attributions — attributing behavior to environmental factors such as task difficulty, luck, or social pressure.

Internal vs. External Attribution

Internal (dispositional): "She failed the exam because she's lazy." The cause is located within the person.
External (situational): "She failed the exam because it was unfairly difficult." The cause is located in the environment.

Harold Kelley's Covariation Model

Kelley (1967) proposed that when we have information about a person's behavior over time, we use three types of information to make attributions:

Kelley's Three Dimensions

Consensus: Do other people behave the same way in this situation? (High = everyone laughs at the comedian; Low = only this person laughs)
Distinctiveness: Does this person behave differently in other situations? (High = she only laughs at this comedian; Low = she laughs at every comedian)
Consistency: Does this person behave the same way in this situation over time? (High = she always laughs at this comedian; Low = she only laughed this once)

PatternConsensusDistinctivenessConsistencyAttribution
External (stimulus)HighHighHigh"The comedian is really funny"
Internal (person)LowLowHigh"She laughs at everything"
CircumstantialLowHighLow"Something unusual happened"
EPPP-Style Application

A supervisor reports that Employee X has been late three days this week. No other employees are late (low consensus), Employee X is late for everything (low distinctiveness), and Employee X is always late (high consistency). This pattern — low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency — leads to an internal attribution: "Employee X is chronically irresponsible."

Kelley, H. H. (1967). Attribution theory in social psychology. Nebraska Symposium on Motivation, 15, 192–238.
prev_last_paragraph: This chapter covers the foundational theories of attribution, the systematic biases that distort social judgment, and the cognitive structures (schemas, stereotypes) that shape how we perceive and remember information about others.

heading_text: Adverse Impact and the Four-Fifths Rule
section_html:
Adverse Impact and the Four-Fifths Rule

Adverse impact occurs when a selection procedure results in a substantially different selection rate for members of a protected group compared to the group with the highest selection rate.

The Four-Fifths (80%) Rule

The four-fifths rule, established in the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (1978), provides a practical measure of adverse impact:

If the selection rate for a protected group is less than 4/5 (80%) of the rate for the group with the highest selection rate, adverse impact is indicated.

Formula: Selection rate of protected group / Selection rate of majority group < .80 = adverse impact

Example: Calculating Adverse Impact

An employer tests 100 White applicants and hires 60 (60% selection rate). The same employer tests 50 Black applicants and hires 20 (40% selection rate).

Adverse impact ratio = 40% / 60% = .667 (66.7%)

Since .667 is less than .80, adverse impact is indicated. The employer would need to demonstrate the test is job-related and consistent with business necessity.

EPPP Key Concept

The four-fifths rule is a guideline, not a strict legal standard. Courts also consider statistical significance tests and practical significance. If adverse impact is found, the burden shifts to the employer to demonstrate job-relatedness (validity). Even if validity is demonstrated, the plaintiff can still prevail by showing that an equally valid alternative with less adverse impact exists.
prev_last_paragraph: The Taylor-Russell tables provide an alternative approach, showing the proportion of successful employees expected when using a selection test, given the test's validity, the selection ratio, and the base rate of success (the proportion who would succeed without the test). Utility is greatest when the validity is high, the selection ratio is low, and the base rate is moderate (around .50).

heading_text: The Four Lobes of the Cerebral Cortex
section_html:
The Four Lobes of the Cerebral Cortex

The cerebral cortex is the outermost layer of the brain, responsible for higher cognitive functions including reasoning, language, and voluntary movement. It is organized into four major lobes, each with distinct functional specializations that are heavily tested on the EPPP.

Frontal Lobe

The frontal lobe occupies the anterior portion of each hemisphere, extending from the central sulcus posteriorly to the frontal pole anteriorly. It contains the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), which controls voluntary movement on the contralateral side of the body. The prefrontal cortex is responsible for executive functions including planning, working memory, impulse control, cognitive flexibility, and social judgment.

Broca's Area (Brodmann areas 44 & 45):

Located in the left inferior frontal gyrus, Broca's area is critical for speech production and language expression. Damage produces Broca's aphasia (expressive/nonfluent aphasia), characterized by effortful, telegraphic speech with preserved comprehension. Patients can understand language but struggle to produce it fluently.

Parietal Lobe

The parietal lobe lies posterior to the central sulcus and is bounded inferiorly by the lateral sulcus. It contains the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), which processes touch, pressure, temperature, and proprioception from the contralateral body. The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) plays a key role in reading and arithmetic; damage can produce alexia and anomia.

Temporal Lobe

The temporal lobe is located beneath the lateral sulcus and contains the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus). It is essential for auditory processing, language comprehension, and memory formation (via the hippocampus).

Wernicke's Area (Brodmann area 22):

Located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, Wernicke's area is responsible for language comprehension. Damage produces Wernicke's aphasia (receptive/fluent aphasia), characterized by fluent but meaningless speech (word salad) with severely impaired comprehension.

Occipital Lobe

The occipital lobe occupies the posterior pole of the brain and contains the primary visual cortex (V1, Brodmann area 17). It processes visual information from the contralateral visual field. Damage to V1 can produce cortical blindness, while damage to association areas can cause visual agnosia.

Storage: Retaining Information

Storage refers to maintaining encoded information over time. The dominant model of memory storage distinguishes three systems based on duration and capacity.

The Atkinson-Shiffrin Model (1968)

Also called the modal model or multi-store model, this framework proposes three sequential stages of memory processing:

FeatureSensory MemoryShort-Term MemoryLong-Term Memory
Duration0.25-4 seconds15-30 seconds (without rehearsal)Potentially unlimited
CapacityLarge (all sensory input)7 +/- 2 items (Miller, 1956)Essentially unlimited
EncodingModality-specificPrimarily acousticPrimarily semantic
ForgettingRapid decayDecay and displacementRetrieval failure, interference

Sensory Memory

The brief retention of sensory information. Iconic memory (visual) lasts approximately 0.5 seconds and was demonstrated by Sperling's (1960) partial-report procedure. Echoic memory (auditory) persists for 3-4 seconds.

Short-Term Memory (STM)

A limited-capacity store that holds information for brief periods. George Miller (1956) established the capacity of STM at 7 plus or minus 2 items. Capacity can be expanded through chunking, the process of grouping individual items into larger meaningful units.

Long-Term Memory (LTM)

The relatively permanent and essentially limitless storage system. Transfer from STM to LTM is facilitated by rehearsal, elaboration, and meaningful processing. LTM is divided into two major subsystems:

  • Explicit (declarative) memory: Conscious recollection of facts and events
    • Episodic memory: Personal experiences and events (Tulving, 1972)
    • Semantic memory: General knowledge and facts about the world
  • Implicit (nondeclarative) memory: Memory without conscious awareness
    • Procedural memory: Motor skills and habits (e.g., riding a bicycle)
    • Priming: Facilitated processing of a stimulus due to prior exposure
    • Classical conditioning: Learned associations between stimuli

Working Memory (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974)

Baddeley's working memory model replaced the unitary concept of STM with a multicomponent system that actively manipulates information rather than passively holding it:

  • Central executive: An attentional control system that directs focus, coordinates the subsystems, and manages cognitive resources. It has limited capacity and is modality-free.
  • Phonological loop: Maintains and rehearses verbal and acoustic information. Consists of a phonological store (the "inner ear") and an articulatory rehearsal process (the "inner voice"). Explains the word-length effect (shorter words are recalled better because they can be rehearsed faster).
  • Visuospatial sketchpad: Maintains and manipulates visual and spatial information (the "inner eye"). Used in navigation, mental imagery, and spatial reasoning.
  • Episodic buffer (added 2000): Integrates information from the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into unified, coherent episodes. Serves as a limited-capacity temporary store.

Clinical Significance: Working memory deficits are observed in ADHD, schizophrenia, traumatic brain injury, and age-related cognitive decline. Neuroimaging consistently implicates the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in working memory tasks.
prev_last_paragraph: EPPP Application: A student who studies in a quiet room will recall material better when tested in a similar quiet environment. Similarly, material learned while in a particular mood is best recalled in that same mood (Bower, 1981).

section_html:
Attention Models & Selective Processing

Attention determines which of the vast amount of incoming sensory information reaches conscious awareness and receives further processing. A central debate in cognitive psychology concerns where in the processing stream selection occurs — early (before meaning is extracted) or late (after full semantic analysis). The major models of attention are frequently tested on the EPPP.

Broadbent's Filter Model (Early Selection)

Broadbent's Filter Model (1958):

Donald Broadbent proposed the first formal model of selective attention. In this early selection model, all sensory information enters a sensory buffer where it is briefly held. A selective filter then allows only one channel of information (selected based on physical characteristics such as location, pitch, or loudness) to pass through to higher-level semantic processing. Unattended information is completely blocked at the filter and never reaches awareness or meaning extraction. Broadbent's model was supported by dichotic listening experiments in which participants could report the content of an attended ear but almost nothing from the unattended ear.

Treisman's Attenuation Model

Treisman's Attenuation Model (1964):

Anne Treisman modified Broadbent's model to account for findings that some unattended information does get through. In Treisman's attenuation model, the filter does not completely block unattended information but instead attenuates (turns down) it — like lowering the volume rather than switching it off. Highly relevant stimuli (e.g., one's own name, danger signals) have permanently lowered activation thresholds and can break through even when attenuated. This explains the cocktail party effect — the ability to detect your own name spoken in an unattended conversation at a noisy party, even though you were not consciously monitoring that conversation.

Deutsch-Norman Late Selection Model

Deutsch and Deutsch (1963), later refined by Norman (1968), proposed a late selection model in which all incoming information is fully processed for meaning (semantically analyzed), and selection occurs only at the response/awareness stage. According to this model, the bottleneck is not in perception but in the decision about what to act on or remember. This explains how people can be influenced by the meaning of unattended messages without being consciously aware of them.

Lavie's Perceptual Load Theory

Lavie's Perceptual Load Theory (1995):

Nilli Lavie proposed an integrative framework that resolves the early-vs.-late selection debate. According to perceptual load theory, whether selection occurs early or late depends on the perceptual load (processing demands) of the attended task. Under high perceptual load (complex, demanding tasks that consume all available processing capacity), selection occurs early — there is no spare capacity to process distractors. Under low perceptual load (simple tasks with spare capacity), unattended information is processed automatically, and selection occurs late. This theory is supported by neuroimaging studies showing reduced neural responses to distractors during high-load tasks.

Posner's Spotlight Model

Michael Posner (1980) proposed that spatial attention operates like a spotlight that can be directed to different regions of the visual field. Attention can be shifted overtly (with eye movements) or covertly (without moving the eyes). Posner identified three component operations of spatial attention: disengaging from the current focus, shifting to the new location, and engaging at the new location. Different brain regions mediate each operation: the posterior parietal cortex is involved in disengaging, the superior colliculus in shifting, and the pulvinar (thalamus) in engaging. Damage to the right parietal lobe produces hemispatial neglect, a dramatic failure to disengage attention from ipsilesional space and attend to contralateral stimuli.

Feature Integration Theory

Feature Integration Theory (Treisman & Gelade, 1980):

This influential theory proposes two stages of visual processing. In the preattentive stage, basic visual features (color, shape, orientation, size, motion) are processed automatically, in parallel, and without conscious effort across the entire visual field. In the focused attention stage, attention is required to bind these individual features together into coherent object representations. Without focused attention, features from different objects can be incorrectly combined, producing illusory conjunctions — for example, incorrectly perceiving a red circle and a blue square as a "red square." This theory explains why a unique feature (e.g., a red item among green items) "pops out" effortlessly in visual search, but searching for a conjunction of features (e.g., a red circle among red squares and green circles) requires slow, serial, attention-demanding search.

Change Blindness & Inattentional Blindness

Two striking phenomena demonstrate the limitations of attention and conscious awareness:

  • Inattentional blindness (Mack & Rock, 1998; Simons & Chabris, 1999): The failure to perceive a clearly visible stimulus when attention is directed elsewhere. In the famous "invisible gorilla" experiment, approximately 50% of observers failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through a basketball game when they were counting passes. This demonstrates that attention, not just visual acuity, is necessary for conscious perception.
  • Change blindness (Rensink, O'Regan, & Clark, 1997): The failure to detect large changes in a visual scene when the change coincides with a brief visual disruption (e.g., a flicker, a saccade, or a cut in a film). Change blindness reveals that we do not maintain a detailed, moment-to-moment representation of the entire visual scene — our sense of a complete visual world is, in part, an illusion constructed by the brain.
Clinical Relevance:

Attentional deficits are a core feature of many psychological disorders tested on the EPPP. ADHD involves impairments in sustained attention and executive control of attention. Hemispatial neglect following right parietal stroke represents a dramatic failure of spatial attention (Posner's disengage operation). Anxiety disorders involve attentional bias toward threat-related stimuli, which can be measured with the dot-probe task. Understanding the theoretical models of attention provides the conceptual framework for understanding these clinical presentations.

EPPP Application:

A question might describe a dichotic listening task where a participant shadows (repeats) a message in one ear but still notices their own name in the unattended ear. The best explanation is Treisman's attenuation model (not Broadbent's filter model, which predicts the name would be completely blocked). If the question describes a participant who fails to notice a large, clearly visible stimulus because they were focused on a demanding task, the answer involves inattentional blindness. If the question asks why a simple visual search is fast but a conjunction search is slow, the answer is Feature Integration Theory.

Broadbent, D. E. (1958). Perception and Communication. London: Pergamon Press.
Treisman, A. M. (1964). Selective attention in man. British Medical Bulletin, 20(1), 12-16.
Treisman, A. M., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.
Lavie, N. (1995). Perceptual load as a necessary condition for selective attention. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 21(3), 451-468.
Simons, D. J., & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.
prev_last_paragraph: Bottom-up processing (data-driven) begins with sensory input and builds up to perception without influence from prior knowledge. Top-down processing (concept-driven) uses prior knowledge, expectations, and context to interpret sensory input. Most perception involves an interaction of both. Top-down processing explains why context allows you to read words with missing letters, why ambiguous stimuli are perceived differently depending on expectations, and why cultural background influences perception.

heading_text: Fixed vs. Flexible Battery and Process Approaches
section_html:
Fixed vs. Flexible Battery and Process Approaches

Fixed Battery Approach:

Administers the same comprehensive set of tests to all patients (e.g., Halstead-Reitan). Advantages: standardization, normative comparison, comprehensive coverage. Disadvantages: time-intensive, may include tests irrelevant to the referral question.

Flexible (Hypothesis-Testing) Battery Approach:

Selects tests based on the specific referral question, patient history, and emerging findings during evaluation. Advantages: efficient, tailored to individual needs. Disadvantages: relies heavily on clinician expertise, less standardized.

The Boston Process Approach (Kaplan)

Edith Kaplan's process approach emphasizes qualitative analysis of how a patient arrives at a response, not just whether the response is correct. For example, on Block Design, the process approach examines the patient's strategy (e.g., broken configurations suggesting parietal dysfunction), time to completion, and error types. This approach can reveal lateralized deficits and specific cognitive processes that quantitative scores alone may miss.

Clinical Integration:

Contemporary neuropsychological practice typically blends approaches: a core set of standardized measures supplemented by hypothesis-driven additional tests, with qualitative process observations integrated throughout. The referral question, patient demographics, and available time guide the specific battery composition.

Effort and Symptom Validity Testing

Assessing the validity of test performance is essential in neuropsychological evaluation, particularly in forensic and disability contexts. Performance validity tests (PVTs) detect suboptimal effort or exaggeration of cognitive impairment:

  • Test of Memory Malingering (TOMM): 50-item visual recognition memory test. Even individuals with severe cognitive impairment typically perform above chance. Scores below 45/50 on Trial 2 suggest insufficient effort.
  • Word Memory Test (WMT): Assesses effort using a paired-associate learning paradigm. Includes immediate recognition, delayed recognition, and consistency measures.
  • Embedded validity indicators: Many standard neuropsychological tests include built-in effort measures. For example, the Reliable Digit Span (RDS) from WAIS-IV Digit Span — scores below 7 suggest possible insufficient effort.
Base Rate of Invalid Performance:

Research suggests that approximately 25-30% of evaluees in forensic and disability settings produce invalid performance on effort measures. In clinical (non-litigation) contexts, the base rate is lower (approximately 5-10%). Current best practice guidelines recommend that at least one standalone PVT and multiple embedded validity indicators be administered in every neuropsychological evaluation.
prev_last_paragraph: The BNT (Kaplan et al., 1983) assesses confrontation naming ability by presenting 60 line drawings of increasing difficulty. The examinee names each picture, with semantic and phonemic cues provided for items not spontaneously named. Impaired naming (anomia) is a hallmark of aphasia and is commonly seen in Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative conditions.

section_html:
Clinical Applications

Classical conditioning principles underlie several evidence-based treatments, particularly for anxiety disorders:

Systematic Desensitization

Developed by Joseph Wolpe (1958), systematic desensitization uses counterconditioning to treat phobias. The procedure involves:

  1. Training the client in relaxation techniques
  2. Constructing a fear hierarchy from least to most anxiety-provoking
  3. Pairing each hierarchy item with relaxation (reciprocal inhibition)
  4. Progressing through the hierarchy until the most feared item can be imagined while relaxed

Exposure Therapy

Modern exposure-based treatments emphasize extinction learning rather than counterconditioning. Prolonged exposure to feared stimuli without the feared outcome allows extinction of the fear response (Craske et al., 2014). Key principles include:

  • Exposure must be prolonged enough for fear reduction to occur
  • Multiple contexts enhance generalization of extinction
  • Variability in exposure parameters may enhance long-term outcomes
  • Cognitive changes (expectancy violation) may be more important than within-session fear reduction
Craske, M. G., Treanor, M., Conway, C. C., Zbozinek, T., & Vervliet, B. (2014). Maximizing exposure therapy: An inhibitory learning approach. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 58, 10-23. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brat.2014.04.006
prev_last_paragraph: Siegel's research explains why many drug overdoses occur when users take their typical dose in unfamiliar environments. The novel context lacks the conditioned cues that normally trigger compensatory responses, resulting in an unexpectedly powerful drug effect. This underscores the importance of contextual factors in substance use treatment.

section_html:
Factors Affecting Validity Coefficients

Several factors can attenuate or inflate validity coefficients, making it important to interpret them in context.

The validity coefficient between a predictor and a criterion is a correlation, and like any correlation, its square yields a coefficient of determination (r²) that indicates the proportion of variance in one variable accounted for by the other. This value is central to understanding the practical meaning of any validity coefficient.

Coefficient of Determination in Validity

When a predictor has a criterion-related validity coefficient of r, the value r² represents the percentage of variability in criterion scores that is explained by variability in predictor scores. The remaining variance (1 − r²) reflects the influence of other factors, measurement error, and unexplained variability.

Example: Interpreting a Validity Coefficient of .80

Suppose a structured interview protocol correlates .80 with subsequent job performance ratings. Squaring this coefficient: .80² = .64. This means that 64% of the variability in job performance scores can be accounted for by variability in interview scores. The remaining 36% of criterion variance is due to other influences—motivation, organizational factors, life circumstances, or error in the performance ratings themselves. Although a validity coefficient of .80 is exceptionally high (and rarely achieved in practice), recognizing that even this strong relationship leaves more than a third of criterion variance unexplained underscores why multiple predictors and holistic assessment strategies are typically preferred.

Validity Coefficient (r) Variance Explained (r²) Variance Unexplained (1 − r²)
.30 9% 91%
.50 25% 75%
.70 49% 51%
.80 64% 36%

When evaluating validity evidence, always consider both the raw correlation and the squared value. A validity coefficient that appears strong (e.g., .50) may account for only 25% of criterion variance, highlighting the gap between statistical significance and practical explanatory power.

When interpreting individual test scores, clinicians frequently construct confidence intervals around obtained scores to account for measurement error. The confidence interval is built using the standard error of measurement (SEM), which reflects the average amount by which observed scores deviate from true scores. For a 95% confidence interval, the obtained score is bounded by approximately ±1.96 × SEM (often rounded to ±2 × SEM for practical purposes).

Example: Constructing a 95% Confidence Interval for an IQ Score

A middle school student earns a full-scale IQ score of 105 on an intelligence test with a mean of 100, a standard deviation of 15, and an SEM of 3. To build the 95% confidence interval:

Lower bound = 105 − (1.96 × 3) = 105 − 5.88 ≈ 99
Upper bound = 105 + (1.96 × 3) = 105 + 5.88 ≈ 111

The clinician can state with 95% confidence that the student's true IQ score falls between 99 and 111. Notice that although the obtained score is 105, the interval spans from the average range into the high-average range, reminding us that a single score is an estimate rather than a precise value. This information is critical for high-stakes decisions such as gifted program eligibility or special education classification, where a few points can determine placement.

Confidence intervals are directly relevant to validity studies because unreliability in either the predictor or criterion introduces error that attenuates observed validity coefficients. Understanding SEM and the imprecision of individual scores provides the foundation for appreciating why corrections for attenuation and other statistical adjustments are necessary when evaluating criterion-related validity evidence.

Example: 95% Confidence Interval for a Predicted Score

An employer uses an aptitude test to predict job performance. One applicant receives a predicted performance score of 75. The standard deviation of job performance scores across all employees is 6, and the standard error of estimate (SEest) for the regression equation is 4. To construct a 95% confidence interval around this prediction:

CI = 75 ± (1.96)(4) = 75 ± 7.84

Rounding appropriately, this yields a range of approximately 67 to 83. The employer can be 95% confident that this applicant's actual job performance score falls within this band. Notice that the SEest of 4 is smaller than the criterion SD of 6 — this difference reflects the predictive value of the test. If the test had no validity whatsoever, the SEest would equal the criterion SD, and the confidence interval would be wider. The stronger the validity of the predictor, the smaller the SEest relative to the SD, and the more precisely we can forecast individual outcomes.

Confidence Intervals for Predicted Scores

When using regression to forecast criterion performance, the predicted score (Ŷ) is a point estimate surrounded by uncertainty. The standard error of estimate (SEest) quantifies the average amount by which actual criterion scores deviate from their predicted values. Confidence intervals around a predicted score are constructed using the same logic as other confidence intervals: the predicted value plus or minus a critical z-value multiplied by the SEest.

Confidence Interval for a Predicted Score

CI = Ŷ ± (z)(SEest)

For a 95% CI, z = 1.96 (commonly rounded to 2)
For a 99% CI, z = 2.58 (commonly rounded to 2.58)

The width of this interval reflects the precision of prediction. A smaller SEest yields narrower intervals and more useful predictions. The confidence level selected determines how much certainty we require: a 99% interval is wider than a 95% interval because greater certainty demands a broader range.

Example: 99% Confidence Interval

An industrial-organizational psychologist uses a selection test to predict job performance. For a particular applicant, the predicted performance score is 80, the criterion standard deviation is 7, and the SEest is 3. To build a 99% confidence interval:

CI = 80 ± (2.58)(3) = 80 ± 7.74

This yields an approximate range of 72.26 to 87.74. Rounding to convenient values, we can say with 99% confidence that the applicant's true job performance score falls roughly between 71 and 89. Note that the standard deviation of the criterion (7) describes overall variability in performance scores, whereas the SEest (3) — which is always smaller when the predictor has validity — reflects the residual variability after prediction. It is the SEest, not the SD, that is used to form confidence intervals around predicted scores.

Standard Error of Estimate

When regression is used to forecast criterion performance from test scores, each predicted score is an estimate subject to error. The standard error of estimate (SEest, also symbolized as SY·X) quantifies the average amount by which actual criterion scores deviate from the values predicted by the regression equation. It serves the same conceptual purpose for predicted scores that the standard error of measurement serves for observed scores: it allows construction of a confidence interval around the predicted criterion value.

The formula for the standard error of estimate is:

SEest = SDY √(1 − r²xy)

where SDY is the standard deviation of criterion scores and rxy is the validity coefficient. As the validity coefficient increases, the standard error of estimate decreases, reflecting greater precision in prediction. When validity is zero, SEest equals the full standard deviation of the criterion, meaning the regression equation provides no improvement over simply guessing the mean. When validity is perfect (r = 1.0), SEest equals zero—predicted scores match actual scores exactly.

Example

A graduate admissions test has a validity coefficient of r = .50 for predicting first-year GPA, and the GPA standard deviation is 0.60. The standard error of estimate is 0.60 × √(1 − .25) = 0.60 × .866 = 0.52. For an applicant whose predicted GPA is 3.20, a 68% confidence interval extends from 2.68 to 3.72 (3.20 ± 0.52). A 95% confidence interval would span approximately ±1.04 points around the predicted value (3.20 ± 2 × 0.52), or 2.16 to 4.24. The substantial width of this interval reflects the moderate level of predictive accuracy.

Clinical Note

The standard error of estimate reminds practitioners that predicted scores are probabilistic, not deterministic. High-stakes decisions should never rest solely on a single point prediction; the confidence band around that prediction should inform how much weight to assign the forecast, especially when validity is modest.

Restriction of Range

Restriction of range occurs when the variability of scores in the validation sample is less than in the applicant population. This commonly happens in predictive validity studies when only those who score above a cutoff are selected, reducing the range of predictor scores available for validation. Range restriction attenuates the observed validity coefficient.

Range Restriction Example

A company uses a cognitive ability test to select employees, hiring only those who score above the 70th percentile. When validating the test against job performance, only selected employees (those with high scores) are available. The restricted range of test scores reduces the observed validity coefficient. Statistical corrections can estimate what the validity would be in the full applicant population.

Criterion Contamination

Criterion contamination occurs when knowledge of predictor scores influences criterion ratings. If supervisors know employees' test scores, their performance ratings may be biased by this knowledge, artificially inflating the validity coefficient.

Criterion Deficiency

Criterion deficiency occurs when the criterion measure fails to capture all relevant aspects of the outcome domain. A deficient criterion underestimates true validity because the test may validly predict aspects of performance not captured by the criterion.

Unreliability

Unreliability in either the predictor or criterion attenuates the validity coefficient. The correction for attenuation formula estimates what validity would be if both measures were perfectly reliable:

rxy(corrected) = rxy / √(rxx × ryy)
prev_last_paragraph: Concurrent validity is demonstrated when test scores correlate with a criterion measured at approximately the same time. This approach is often used when developing a shorter or more efficient assessment to replace a longer criterion measure, or when establishing that a new test measures the same construct as an established instrument.

section_html:
Base Rates and Selection Ratios

The practical utility of a test depends not only on its validity but also on the base rate and selection ratio.

Base Rate

The base rate is the proportion of people in the population who would succeed on the criterion without selection (or who have the condition being assessed). Base rate affects how much a test can improve upon chance prediction.

Base Rate Effects

  • Very high base rate (e.g., 90%): Most people succeed; test has little room to improve prediction
  • Very low base rate (e.g., 10%): Most people fail/don't have condition; predicting "no" is often correct
  • Moderate base rate (around 50%): Maximum opportunity for test to improve prediction

Selection Ratio

The selection ratio is the proportion of applicants who are selected. A lower selection ratio (selecting fewer applicants) allows for selecting only those with the highest scores, potentially improving outcomes but reducing the number selected.

Taylor-Russell Tables

Taylor and Russell (1939) developed tables showing the expected success rate given different combinations of validity coefficient, base rate, and selection ratio. These tables demonstrate that even tests with modest validity can substantially improve selection outcomes when base rates are moderate and selection ratios are low.
prev_last_paragraph: For example, if a test has a reliability of .64, its validity coefficient cannot exceed √.64 = .80, regardless of how well the construct aligns with the criterion. In practice, validity coefficients are almost always substantially lower than this theoretical ceiling. This principle underscores why adequate reliability is a necessary (though not sufficient) precondition for validity: a measure riddled with measurement error cannot consistently relate to anything external. When evaluating a low validity coefficient, clinicians and researchers should first examine whether poor reliability may be the limiting factor before concluding that the test lacks a meaningful relationship to the criterion.

chapter_title: From Samples to Populations: Inferential Statistics
section_html:
t-Tests

The t-test is used to compare means when the population standard deviation is unknown (which is almost always the case). There are three main types of t-tests:

Independent Samples t-Test

Used to compare means from two different groups (between-subjects design). For example, comparing depression scores between a treatment group and a control group. Assumptions include:

  • Independent observations
  • Normally distributed populations (or large samples)
  • Homogeneity of variance (equal variances in both groups)

Paired Samples t-Test

Used to compare means from the same group at two different times or under two different conditions (within-subjects design). Also called the dependent samples t-test or repeated measures t-test. For example, comparing pre-treatment and post-treatment scores in the same participants.

One-Sample t-Test

Used to compare a sample mean to a known or hypothesized population value. For example, testing whether a sample's IQ differs from the population mean of 100.

Example: Choosing a t-Test

Scenario: A researcher measures anxiety before and after a relaxation intervention in the same 30 participants.

Appropriate test: Paired samples t-test, because the same participants are measured twice (within-subjects design).

Scenario: A researcher compares anxiety scores between 30 participants who received treatment and 30 different participants who received placebo.

Appropriate test: Independent samples t-test, because different participants are in each group (between-subjects design).
prev_last_paragraph: Power analysis is used to determine the sample size needed to achieve adequate power for detecting an effect of a given size. A priori power analysis (conducted before data collection) helps ensure studies are adequately powered. Post hoc power analysis (conducted after finding non-significant results) is generally discouraged because observed power is a direct function of the obtained p-value.

chapter_title: From Samples to Populations: Inferential Statistics
heading_text: Extensions of ANOVA: ANCOVA, MANOVA, and MANCOVA
section_html:
Extensions of ANOVA: ANCOVA, MANOVA, and MANCOVA

Several important extensions of ANOVA address common research situations where the basic ANOVA framework is insufficient. These extensions either add covariates, accommodate multiple dependent variables, or both (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2019).

Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)

ANCOVA combines ANOVA with regression by including one or more covariates—continuous variables that are statistically controlled to reduce error variance and remove the influence of confounding variables. ANCOVA adjusts group means on the DV to account for pre-existing differences on the covariate.

ANCOVA Key Points

  • Purpose: Statistically control for confounding variables that cannot be controlled experimentally
  • Covariate requirement: The covariate must be measured before treatment (pre-treatment) so it is not affected by the independent variable
  • Effect: Reduces within-group error variance, increasing statistical power
  • Assumption: Homogeneity of regression slopes—the relationship between the covariate and the DV must be similar across groups

ANCOVA Example

A researcher compares the effectiveness of three therapy approaches on post-treatment anxiety scores. Because groups may differ in pre-treatment anxiety, the researcher uses pre-treatment anxiety as a covariate in an ANCOVA. This statistically adjusts post-treatment means to reflect what they would be if all groups had started with equal pre-treatment anxiety levels.

Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA)

MANOVA extends ANOVA to situations with multiple dependent variables measured simultaneously. Rather than running separate ANOVAs for each DV (which inflates Type I error), MANOVA tests whether groups differ on a linear combination of the DVs in a single omnibus test.

MANOVA Key Points

  • Purpose: Compare groups on multiple DVs simultaneously while controlling familywise Type I error rate
  • Test statistics: Wilks' Lambda (most commonly reported; based on ratio of determinants), Pillai's Trace (most robust to violations of assumptions), Hotelling's Trace, Roy's Largest Root
  • Assumptions: Multivariate normality, homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices (Box's M test), independence of observations
  • Follow-up analyses: If the omnibus MANOVA is significant, follow up with discriminant function analysis (preferred, as it accounts for DV intercorrelations) or individual ANOVAs on each DV with Bonferroni correction

MANOVA Example

A researcher compares two therapy groups on three outcome measures simultaneously: depression, anxiety, and quality of life. Running three separate ANOVAs would inflate the Type I error rate (approximately 1 - .95^3 = .14 rather than .05). MANOVA tests all three DVs in one analysis, maintaining the overall alpha at .05. The researcher reports Wilks' Lambda and, if significant, conducts follow-up analyses to determine which DVs contribute to the group difference.

Multivariate Analysis of Covariance (MANCOVA)

MANCOVA combines the features of both MANOVA and ANCOVA—it analyzes multiple dependent variables simultaneously while statistically controlling for one or more covariates. This is used when a researcher has both multiple outcome measures and pre-existing differences that need to be adjusted for.

When to Use Each Extension

  • ANCOVA: One DV + need to control for a covariate (e.g., comparing treatment groups on post-test scores while controlling for pre-test)
  • MANOVA: Multiple DVs + no covariates needed (e.g., comparing treatment groups on depression, anxiety, and functioning simultaneously)
  • MANCOVA: Multiple DVs + need to control for a covariate (e.g., comparing treatment groups on multiple outcomes while controlling for baseline severity)
prev_last_paragraph: When ANOVA indicates significant differences, post hoc tests are used to determine which specific groups differ. Common post hoc tests include:

section_html:
Escape and Avoidance Learning

Escape and avoidance learning are important forms of negative reinforcement that help explain the maintenance of anxiety disorders and other clinical phenomena.

Escape Learning

Escape learning occurs when an organism learns to perform a behavior that terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus. The removal of the aversive stimulus serves as negative reinforcement for the escape behavior. For example, taking aspirin to relieve a headache is escape behavior - the behavior is reinforced by termination of the pain.

Avoidance Learning

Avoidance learning occurs when an organism learns to perform a behavior that prevents an aversive stimulus from occurring. The avoidance response is made before the aversive stimulus is presented, based on warning signals (discriminative stimuli).

Two-Factor Theory of Avoidance

Mowrer's (1947) two-factor theory explains avoidance learning through a combination of classical and operant conditioning:

  1. Factor 1 (Classical conditioning): A neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) for fear through pairing with an aversive unconditioned stimulus
  2. Factor 2 (Operant conditioning): The avoidance response is negatively reinforced by reduction of the conditioned fear

This theory explains why avoidance behavior is so resistant to extinction - the organism never remains in the presence of the feared stimulus long enough for extinction to occur.

Clinical Implications: Anxiety Maintenance

Two-factor theory provides a behavioral account of anxiety disorder maintenance. Avoidance prevents exposure to feared situations, thereby preventing extinction of conditioned fear. This explains why exposure therapy, which prevents avoidance and allows extinction to occur, is effective for anxiety disorders. The theory also explains why reassurance-seeking and safety behaviors maintain anxiety (Salkovskis, 1991).

Mowrer, O. H. (1947). On the dual nature of learning: A re-interpretation of "conditioning" and "problem-solving." Harvard Educational Review, 17, 102-148.
prev_last_paragraph: As we move forward, keep in mind that stimulus control helps explain not just simple responses to environmental cues but also more complex learning phenomena. Next, we'll explore how organisms learn to respond to aversive stimuli — specifically, how escape and avoidance behaviors develop and are maintained.

section_html:
Clinical Applications

Operant conditioning principles form the foundation for numerous evidence-based interventions across clinical, educational, and organizational settings.

Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA)

Applied Behavior Analysis is the application of operant conditioning principles to improve socially significant behaviors. ABA is characterized by its focus on observable behavior, reliance on data-based decision making, and emphasis on socially important outcomes. It has become the primary evidence-based treatment for autism spectrum disorder (Lovaas, 1987).

Behavioral Activation

Behavioral activation for depression is based on operant principles. Depression is conceptualized as a state of low positive reinforcement - depressed individuals engage in fewer pleasurable activities and receive less positive reinforcement. Treatment involves systematically increasing engagement in reinforcing activities, breaking the cycle of withdrawal and reduced reinforcement (Martell et al., 2010).

Contingency Management

Contingency management interventions provide tangible reinforcers contingent on evidence of desired behavior change (typically verified drug abstinence). These interventions have demonstrated robust efficacy for substance use disorders, particularly stimulant use disorders where pharmacological treatments are limited (Higgins et al., 2004).

Example: Voucher-Based Contingency Management

In voucher-based contingency management for cocaine dependence, patients receive vouchers exchangeable for retail goods contingent on cocaine-negative urine specimens. Voucher values typically start low and increase with consecutive negative specimens, with a reset contingency for positive specimens. Meta-analyses demonstrate significant effects on drug abstinence outcomes.

Functional Behavior Assessment

Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA) is a process for identifying the environmental variables that maintain problem behavior. By identifying the function of behavior (what reinforces it), clinicians can develop function-based interventions that address the maintaining contingencies rather than simply suppressing behavior (Hanley et al., 2003).

Common functions of problem behavior include:

  • Attention: Behavior maintained by social reinforcement
  • Escape: Behavior maintained by negative reinforcement (removal of demands)
  • Access to tangibles: Behavior maintained by access to preferred items or activities
  • Automatic reinforcement: Behavior maintained by sensory consequences independent of social mediation
Hanley, G. P., Iwata, B. A., & McCord, B. E. (2003). Functional analysis of problem behavior: A review. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 36(2), 147-185.
prev_last_paragraph: Two-factor theory provides a behavioral account of anxiety disorder maintenance. Avoidance prevents exposure to feared situations, thereby preventing extinction of conditioned fear. This explains why exposure therapy, which prevents avoidance and allows extinction to occur, is effective for anxiety disorders. The theory also explains why reassurance-seeking and safety behaviors maintain anxiety (Salkovskis, 1991).

section_html:
Classical Test Theory

Classical Test Theory provides the theoretical foundation for understanding reliability. The core assumption is that any observed score (X) consists of two components: a true score (T) and error (E).

Classical Test Theory Formula

X = T + E

Where:

  • X = Observed score (what we measure)
  • T = True score (the person's actual ability)
  • E = Error (random measurement error)

Assumptions of Classical Test Theory

  • The mean error of measurement equals zero across repeated testing
  • True scores and error scores are uncorrelated
  • Error scores on one test are uncorrelated with error scores on another test
  • Error scores are uncorrelated with true scores on other tests

Reliability as True Score Variance

The reliability coefficient can be expressed as:

rxx = σ²T / σ²X = 1 - (σ²E / σ²X)

A reliability coefficient of .80 means that 80% of the observed score variance is true score variance, while 20% is error variance.
prev_last_paragraph: In Classical Test Theory (CTT), reliability is conceptualized as the proportion of observed score variance attributable to true score variance. Mathematically, the reliability coefficient (rxx) represents the ratio of true score variance to observed score variance (Lord & Novick, 1968). This deceptively simple ratio — true variance divided by total variance — forms the backbone of how psychologists evaluate measurement quality, and it gives rise to the several different methods of estimating reliability that we will explore throughout this chapter. But before we can fully appreciate those methods, we need to understand the formal assumptions of Classical Test Theory itself.

section_html:
Types of Reliability

Different types of reliability assess different sources of measurement error. The appropriate type depends on the nature of the test and how it will be used (AERA et al., 2014).

Test-Retest Reliability

Test-retest reliability (also called temporal stability) assesses the consistency of scores across time. The same test is administered to the same individuals on two occasions, and the correlation between scores indicates stability.

Test-Retest Reliability

  • Method: Administer same test twice; correlate scores
  • Source of error: Time sampling (changes in examinees over time)
  • Considerations: Interval between testings, memory/practice effects, true changes in the construct

Optimal Testing Interval

The appropriate interval depends on the construct being measured:

  • Shorter intervals (days to weeks): Minimize true change but increase practice effects
  • Longer intervals (months): Reduce practice effects but allow more true change
  • Stable traits (intelligence, personality): Longer intervals are appropriate
  • Variable states (mood, anxiety): Very short intervals or alternative methods

Alternate (Parallel) Forms Reliability

Alternate forms reliability assesses consistency across different versions of the same test. Two equivalent forms are administered to the same individuals, and the correlation between forms indicates reliability. This method controls for memory effects and provides evidence of content sampling consistency.

Alternate Forms Example

A publisher develops Form A and Form B of an achievement test, each with different items measuring the same content domain. Students take Form A one week and Form B the next. A correlation of .85 between forms indicates good alternate forms reliability, suggesting the two versions measure the same construct consistently.

For forms to be truly parallel, they must have equal means, equal variances, and equal correlations with other measures. In practice, this is difficult to achieve, so most alternate forms are better described as "equivalent" rather than strictly parallel.

Internal Consistency Reliability

Internal consistency assesses the homogeneity of items within a single test administration. It indicates the extent to which items measure the same construct and is the most commonly reported type of reliability.

Split-Half Reliability

The test is divided into two halves (typically odd vs. even items), and the correlation between halves is calculated. Because each half is only half as long as the full test, the Spearman-Brown formula is used to estimate the reliability of the full-length test.

Spearman-Brown Prophecy Formula

rxx = (2 × rhh) / (1 + rhh)

Where rhh is the correlation between the two halves.

For example, if the correlation between halves is .60, the estimated full-test reliability is:

(2 × .60) / (1 + .60) = 1.20 / 1.60 = .75

Cronbach's Alpha (Coefficient Alpha)

Cronbach's alpha (α) is the most widely used measure of internal consistency. It represents the average of all possible split-half reliabilities and indicates how well items hang together as a set. Alpha is appropriate for items with multiple response options (Cronbach, 1951).

Alpha values are interpreted as follows:

Alpha Value Interpretation
≥ .90 Excellent (individual decision-making)
.80 - .89 Good
.70 - .79 Acceptable (research purposes)
.60 - .69 Questionable
< .60 Poor/Unacceptable

Kuder-Richardson Formulas

The Kuder-Richardson formulas are special cases of Cronbach's alpha for dichotomously scored items (correct/incorrect). KR-20 is used when item difficulties vary, while KR-21 assumes equal item difficulties (Kuder & Richardson, 1937).

Limitations of Internal Consistency

  • May be inappropriately high for speeded tests (items are not independently answered)
  • Does not assess stability over time
  • May be artificially inflated by redundant items
  • Not appropriate for multidimensional tests (should be calculated separately for each subscale)

Inter-Rater (Inter-Scorer) Reliability

Inter-rater reliability assesses the consistency of scores assigned by different raters or scorers. This is essential for tests involving subjective judgment, such as essay tests, behavioral observations, projective tests, and structured interviews.

A significant threat to the accuracy of inter-rater reliability estimates is consensual observer drift (sometimes called observer drift or rater drift). This phenomenon occurs when two or more raters who work closely together gradually develop a shared, idiosyncratic interpretation of the scoring criteria that deviates from the original operational definitions. Over time, the raters' scoring systems converge with each other but diverge from the intended scoring standards. Because the raters are drifting in the same direction together, their agreement remains high—or even increases—producing an artificially inflated inter-rater reliability coefficient that does not reflect true scoring accuracy.

The core problem is that high agreement between raters is mistaken for accurate measurement. Two observers may consistently agree on ratings while both systematically misapplying the scoring rubric. This inflated consistency masks a decline in scoring validity. Consensual drift is most likely when raters are trained together and continue to observe or score together over extended periods without independent calibration checks.

Clinical Note

To guard against consensual observer drift, researchers and clinicians should periodically retrain raters against criterion standards ("gold standard" recordings or master-rated exemplars), rotate rater pairings so that observers do not always work alongside the same partner, and include independent reliability checks with outside raters who have not been exposed to the local scoring culture. These strategies help ensure that inter-rater agreement reflects genuine adherence to scoring criteria rather than shared deviation from them.

Methods of Assessment

  • Percent agreement: Simple but does not account for chance agreement
  • Cohen's kappa (κ): Corrects for chance agreement; used for categorical ratings
  • Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC): Used for continuous ratings; accounts for both agreement and consistency

Cohen's Kappa Interpretation

  • κ < .20: Poor agreement
  • κ = .21 - .40: Fair agreement
  • κ = .41 - .60: Moderate agreement
  • κ = .61 - .80: Substantial agreement
  • κ > .80: Almost perfect agreement
prev_last_paragraph: The EPPP itself uses IRT-based scoring. Items are calibrated using IRT models, and examinee scores are estimated on a theta scale. This means the EPPP can draw from a large item bank while maintaining score comparability across administrations. The pass/fail decision is based on a theta cutoff rather than a raw percentage correct, which accounts for differences in item difficulty across test forms.

section_html:
Sampling Methods

The method used to select participants affects the generalizability of research findings. Probability sampling methods give every member of the population a known, nonzero chance of selection, supporting statistical generalization.

Types of Probability Sampling

Method Description Advantage
Simple Random Every member has equal chance of selection Unbiased representation
Stratified Random Population divided into strata; random sampling within each Ensures representation of subgroups
Cluster Randomly select clusters (e.g., schools), sample all within Practical for geographically dispersed populations
Systematic Select every kth member from a list Simple to implement

Nonprobability Sampling

Nonprobability sampling methods do not ensure every member has a chance of selection. These include convenience sampling (readily available participants), purposive sampling (participants selected for specific characteristics), and snowball sampling (participants recruit other participants).
prev_last_paragraph: Mixed designs (also called split-plot designs) include both between-subjects and within-subjects factors. For example, a study might compare two therapy groups (between-subjects) measured at multiple time points (within-subjects).

chapter_title: Measuring What Matters: Content & Construct Validity
section_html:
Relationship Between Reliability and Validity

Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A test cannot measure a construct accurately (be valid) if it does not measure consistently (be reliable). However, a test can be highly reliable while measuring the wrong construct.

Key Relationships

  • Validity cannot exceed the square root of reliability: rxy ≤ √rxx
  • High reliability does not guarantee validity
  • Low reliability limits the maximum possible validity
  • Both reliability and validity are essential for meaningful measurement

Reliability-Validity Relationship

A weight scale might reliably measure weight (high reliability) but would have no validity for measuring intelligence. Conversely, a test with reliability of .64 can have maximum validity of only √.64 = .80, regardless of how well the content represents the intended construct.
prev_last_paragraph: Bias is a statistical/psychometric concept referring to systematic measurement error. Fairness is a broader concept encompassing social values and judgments about appropriate test use. A test can be psychometrically unbiased yet still raise fairness concerns if its use produces adverse impact on protected groups.

chapter_title: Variables, Scales & the Language of Data
section_html:
Skewness and Kurtosis

Real data often deviate from the normal distribution. Two important characteristics describe the shape of distributions: skewness and kurtosis.

Skewness

Skewness refers to the asymmetry of a distribution. In a positively skewed distribution, the tail extends toward higher values (right), and the mean is greater than the median. In a negatively skewed distribution, the tail extends toward lower values (left), and the mean is less than the median.

Skewness Examples

Positive skew: Income distribution (many low-to-moderate incomes, few very high incomes pulling the mean up)

Negative skew: Age at death in developed countries (most people live to old age, with some early deaths pulling the mean down)

Kurtosis

Kurtosis describes the "peakedness" of a distribution and the heaviness of its tails. Leptokurtic distributions are more peaked with heavier tails than normal (positive kurtosis). Platykurtic distributions are flatter with lighter tails (negative kurtosis). Mesokurtic distributions have the same kurtosis as the normal distribution.

Practical Implications

Severe skewness or kurtosis can violate assumptions of parametric statistical tests. Options include:

  • Using nonparametric alternatives
  • Transforming data (log, square root)
  • Using robust statistical methods
  • Reporting median instead of mean for skewed data

chapter_title: Variables, Scales & the Language of Data
section_html:
Percentiles and Percentile Ranks

Percentiles describe scores in terms of their relative position in a distribution.

A percentile rank indicates the percentage of scores in a distribution that fall at or below a given score. A score at the 75th percentile (P75) exceeds 75% of scores in the distribution.

A percentile point (or percentile) is the score at or below which a specified percentage of scores falls. The 75th percentile point is the score that 75% of examinees scored at or below.

Special Percentiles: Quartiles

  • Q1 (25th percentile): First quartile—25% of scores fall below
  • Q2 (50th percentile): Second quartile—the median
  • Q3 (75th percentile): Third quartile—75% of scores fall below
  • Interquartile Range (IQR): Q3 - Q1, contains middle 50% of scores

Interpreting Test Scores

When interpreting psychological test scores, percentile ranks are often more intuitive for clients than standard scores. However, percentile ranks have important limitations:

  • They are not equal-interval—a difference of 10 percentile points near the mean represents fewer raw score points than the same difference at the extremes
  • They cannot be meaningfully averaged or subjected to arithmetic operations
  • They should not be compared across different normative samples
