Dynamic risk factors (criminogenic needs) are modifiable targets for intervention (e.g., substance use, antisocial attitudes, peer associations, employment instability). Effective risk management addresses dynamic factors while acknowledging the baseline risk indicated by static factors.

heading_text: Overview of Clinical and Neuropsychological Tests
section_html:
Overview of Clinical and Neuropsychological Tests

This chapter covers specialized clinical instruments and neuropsychological test batteries that are commonly tested on the EPPP. Unlike the broad cognitive measures (Wechsler, Stanford-Binet) or personality inventories (MMPI, NEO), these instruments target specific clinical functions such as visual-motor integration, cognitive screening, executive functioning, and comprehensive neuropsychological assessment.

EPPP Focus: For neuropsychological tests, the exam typically asks about what each test measures, the populations for which it is used, and key scoring or interpretation features. You are less likely to be asked about specific administration details.

Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test

The Bender Visual Motor Gestalt Test (commonly called the Bender-Gestalt) was originally developed by Lauretta Bender in 1938 based on Gestalt psychology principles from Max Wertheimer. It assesses visual-motor integration by asking examinees to copy geometric designs.

Test Description

  • The original version presents 9 geometric designs one at a time; the examinee copies each design onto blank paper
  • The Bender-Gestalt II (Brannigan & Decker, 2003) updated the instrument with 16 designs, modern norms (ages 4-85+), and supplemental tests (motor and perception tests)
  • Administration takes approximately 5-10 minutes for the copy phase

Scoring Systems

  • Koppitz Developmental Scoring System: Used primarily with children ages 5-11; scores 30 possible errors across categories of distortion, rotation, integration, and perseveration
  • Lacks Scoring System: Designed for adults; identifies 12 essential discriminators of organic brain impairment
  • Bender-Gestalt II Global Scoring System: Uses a 0-4 rating for each design based on overall quality of reproduction

Clinical Uses

  • Screening for visual-motor integration deficits
  • Screening for possible neurological impairment (though sensitivity/specificity is limited)
  • Developmental assessment in children
  • A recall phase (redrawing from memory) can assess visual memory
EPPP Key Point: The Bender-Gestalt is a screening instrument, not a diagnostic tool. Errors such as rotation, fragmentation, perseveration, and collision of figures may suggest neurological impairment but require follow-up with comprehensive neuropsychological testing.

section_html:
Culture-Fair and Culture-Free Testing

The concepts of culture-fair and culture-free testing represent different approaches to minimizing cultural bias in cognitive assessment:

Culture-Free Tests

Culture-free tests aim to be completely independent of cultural influence. This is now widely recognized as an impossible ideal because all cognitive tests are affected to some degree by the examinee's cultural background, educational opportunity, familiarity with testing situations, and test-taking strategies.

Culture-Fair Tests

Culture-fair tests (sometimes called "culture-reduced" tests) attempt to minimize cultural bias without claiming to eliminate it entirely. Strategies include:

  • Using nonverbal stimuli and response formats
  • Reducing language demands in both instructions and responses
  • Using abstract geometric or figural content rather than content tied to specific cultural knowledge
  • Providing practice items to ensure the examinee understands the task format
  • Developing norms that include representative samples of diverse populations

Cattell's Culture Fair Intelligence Test (CFIT)

Raymond Cattell developed the CFIT specifically to measure fluid intelligence while minimizing cultural influence. It uses four subtests: Series, Classifications, Matrices, and Conditions, all using abstract figures. Three difficulty levels (Scales 1, 2, 3) are available for different age ranges and ability levels.

EPPP Critical Point: No test is truly culture-free. Even nonverbal tests show group differences related to cultural factors such as familiarity with testing formats, experience with abstract visual patterns, and motivation to perform in testing situations. The appropriate term is "culture-reduced" or "culture-fair," and clinicians must still consider cultural context when interpreting results.
prev_last_paragraph: The CogAT uses a unique ability profile system that describes the pattern of scores across the three batteries:

section_html:
Nonverbal Assessment: Best Practices

When assessing individuals for whom standard verbal-loaded tests are inappropriate, clinicians should follow these guidelines:

  • Select instruments normed on populations that include the examinee's demographic group
  • Consider whether nonverbal instructions (as in the Leiter-3) are necessary, or whether nonverbal test content with verbal instructions (as in Raven's) is sufficient
  • Use multiple measures rather than a single nonverbal test to get a more comprehensive picture
  • Report results with appropriate caveats about the limitations of nonverbal assessment
  • Recognize that nonverbal IQ scores may underrepresent the abilities of verbally strong individuals
  • Avoid using a single nonverbal screening measure as a definitive measure of intellectual functioning
prev_last_paragraph: Raymond Cattell developed the CFIT specifically to measure fluid intelligence while minimizing cultural influence. It uses four subtests: Series, Classifications, Matrices, and Conditions, all using abstract figures. Three difficulty levels (Scales 1, 2, 3) are available for different age ranges and ability levels.

section_html:
Treatment Planning

Effective treatment planning integrates diagnostic assessment, case formulation, treatment selection, and ongoing monitoring. Key principles include:

Case Formulation

A case formulation is a hypothesis about the causes, precipitants, and maintaining factors of an individual's psychological problems. It goes beyond diagnosis to provide a conceptual framework for treatment. Components typically include:

  • Presenting problems and their functional impact
  • Predisposing factors (e.g., developmental history, genetics, early learning)
  • Precipitating factors (e.g., recent stressors, life transitions)
  • Perpetuating factors (e.g., avoidance patterns, cognitive distortions, environmental reinforcement)
  • Protective factors and strengths

Matching Treatment to Client

Beutler and colleagues developed the Systematic Treatment Selection (STS) model, which identifies patient dimensions that predict differential response to specific treatment characteristics:

  • Problem complexity / chronicity: More complex or chronic problems may require longer-term, insight-oriented approaches
  • Coping style: Internalizers (high self-blame) respond better to insight-oriented treatments; externalizers respond better to symptom-focused, skill-building approaches
  • Resistance level / reactance: Highly resistant clients respond better to nondirective approaches; low-resistance clients respond well to directive approaches
  • Subjective distress: Moderate distress levels optimize treatment engagement; very low or very high distress may impede progress

Stages of Change (Prochaska & DiClemente)

The Transtheoretical Model suggests that interventions should match the client's readiness for change:

  • Precontemplation: Consciousness-raising, motivational interviewing
  • Contemplation: Decisional balance, exploring ambivalence
  • Preparation: Goal setting, commitment enhancement
  • Action: Behavioral strategies, skill building, contingency management
  • Maintenance: Relapse prevention, stimulus control, social support

Exam questions may present orgasmic reconditioning as a distractor option for these other conditions, so it is essential to remember its specific application to deviant arousal patterns.

heading_text: Common Factors and the Therapeutic Alliance
section_html:
Common Factors and the Therapeutic Alliance

Research consistently shows that common factors account for a substantial proportion of therapy outcome variance -- often cited as more predictive than specific technique factors. Key common factors include:

The Therapeutic Alliance

Bordin's (1979) pantheoretical model defines the alliance as consisting of three components:

  1. Agreement on goals: Therapist and client share an understanding of the targets of treatment
  2. Agreement on tasks: Both parties agree on the activities and methods used in therapy
  3. The relational bond: Mutual trust, respect, liking, and attachment between therapist and client
Meta-analytic findings: The alliance-outcome correlation is approximately r = .28 (Horvath et al., 2011), accounting for roughly 7-8% of outcome variance. While this is a modest effect size, the alliance is one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of treatment outcome across orientations.

Other Common Factors

  • Empathy: The therapist's ability to understand the client's experience (r = .28 with outcome)
  • Positive regard / warmth: Unconditional acceptance of the client
  • Congruence / genuineness: The therapist's authenticity in the relationship
  • Client expectations (placebo/hope): The client's belief that therapy will help
  • Extratherapeutic factors: Client variables and life events outside of therapy -- Lambert (1992) estimated these account for approximately 40% of outcome variance

Lambert's Outcome Factors

Lambert (1992) proposed the following estimated contributions to therapeutic outcome:

FactorEstimated Variance
Extratherapeutic change (client/life factors)40%
Common factors (relationship)30%
Expectancy / placebo effects15%
Specific techniques15%
EPPP Note: These percentages are frequently tested. Remember that Lambert's model suggests technique-specific factors account for only about 15% of outcome variance, while extratherapeutic factors contribute the most at 40%. This supports the "common factors" perspective, though it does not negate the importance of ESTs.

heading_text: The Dodo Bird Verdict and Its Critics
section_html:
The Dodo Bird Verdict and Its Critics

The Dodo bird verdict (from Rosenzweig, 1936, and later Luborsky et al., 1975) holds that all bona fide psychotherapies produce roughly equivalent outcomes -- "everybody has won, and all must have prizes." Supporting and critiquing evidence includes:

  • Supporting evidence: Meta-analyses by Wampold (2001) found minimal differences between active treatments when researcher allegiance and other confounds are controlled
  • Opposing evidence: For specific disorders, some treatments show clear superiority (e.g., ERP for OCD, exposure therapy for specific phobias, behavioral treatments for autism spectrum disorder)
  • Middle ground: Most researchers now accept that common factors are powerful, but specific techniques add incremental value for certain conditions
EPPP Exam Tip: The exam may present scenarios asking you to evaluate whether one treatment is superior to another. Remember: across disorders, differences between bona fide treatments are often small, but for specific conditions (especially anxiety disorders), behavioral and exposure-based treatments have demonstrated superiority.
prev_last_paragraph: Consider the clinical implications: without feedback, therapists tend to continue doing what they have been doing, even when it isn't working. The psychological literature on confirmation bias suggests that clinicians, like all humans, tend to notice evidence that confirms their expectations and overlook evidence that contradicts them. FIT disrupts this pattern by putting objective data directly in the therapist's hands. The research is clear that the biggest beneficiaries are not the clients who are already improving — those clients tend to do well regardless — but the ones who are silently deteriorating. For these not-on-track clients, feedback can be the difference between treatment failure and meaningful recovery. As we turn to the next section on the Dodo Bird Verdict, this theme of what actually drives therapeutic change — and whether specific techniques matter more than common processes like monitoring and alliance — takes center stage.

section_html:
Cultural Considerations in Treatment Selection

EBPP requires that treatment selection account for patient cultural context. Key considerations include:

  • Cultural adaptation of ESTs: Research supports that culturally adapted treatments (those modified to account for the client's language, cultural values, and worldview) are more effective for ethnic minority clients than unadapted versions (Griner & Smith, 2006, d = 0.45)
  • Therapist cultural competence: The therapist's ability to understand and work within the client's cultural framework enhances the therapeutic alliance and improves outcomes
  • Client treatment preferences: Racial and ethnic minority clients may have preferences for certain treatment approaches or may be less likely to engage with treatments perceived as culturally incongruent
  • Access and retention: Structural barriers (language, transportation, insurance, stigma) disproportionately affect minority populations and must be considered in treatment planning
EPPP Note: The EBPP model explicitly includes patient characteristics, culture, and preferences as a co-equal component alongside research evidence. This means that the "best" treatment is not simply the most researched one -- it is the one that integrates the strongest evidence with the specific client's context and values.

section_html:
Prescriptive Matching and Treatment Resistance

Research on prescriptive treatment matching has identified several principles for improving outcomes with treatment-resistant clients:

  • Motivational enhancement: For clients low in motivation, beginning with motivational interviewing (MI) before introducing structured treatments improves engagement and outcomes
  • Stepped care: Starting with less intensive interventions and stepping up to more intensive treatments as needed is both cost-effective and clinically sound
  • Alliance rupture repair: Safran and Muran (2000) demonstrated that identifying and repairing alliance ruptures (confrontation ruptures and withdrawal ruptures) is associated with improved outcomes, particularly with difficult-to-engage clients
  • Therapist effects: Some therapists consistently achieve better outcomes than others. Therapist effects account for approximately 5-8% of outcome variance, comparable to or exceeding the contribution of specific techniques

section_html:
Overview of Interest Inventories

Interest inventories are assessment instruments designed to measure an individual's preferences for various activities, occupations, and work environments. They are primarily used in career counseling and vocational guidance. Unlike aptitude or ability tests, interest inventories do not measure what a person can do, but rather what they prefer to do. For the EPPP, you should know the major instruments, their theoretical foundations, and the specific scales and scores they produce.

Interests vs. Aptitudes: Interests refer to what activities a person finds enjoyable or appealing. Aptitudes refer to the capacity to learn or perform a skill. A person may have strong interest in an area without corresponding aptitude (and vice versa). Comprehensive career assessment typically evaluates both.

Holland's RIASEC Model

John Holland's theory of vocational personalities and work environments is the most widely used framework for understanding vocational interests. Holland proposed that both people and work environments can be classified into six types, forming the RIASEC hexagon:

TypeDescriptionExample Occupations
Realistic (R)Prefers hands-on, physical, mechanical, or outdoor activities; values practical solutionsEngineer, mechanic, carpenter, farmer
Investigative (I)Prefers analytical, intellectual, scientific activities; values research and inquiryScientist, physician, mathematician, researcher
Artistic (A)Prefers creative, unstructured, expressive activities; values aesthetics and imaginationArtist, musician, writer, actor, graphic designer
Social (S)Prefers helping, teaching, counseling, and cooperative activities; values interpersonal relationshipsTeacher, counselor, social worker, nurse
Enterprising (E)Prefers leading, persuading, managing, and selling activities; values influence and statusManager, salesperson, lawyer, politician
Conventional (C)Prefers structured, organized, data-management activities; values accuracy and orderAccountant, banker, clerk, office manager

Key Principles of Holland's Theory

  • Congruence: People are most satisfied and productive when their personality type matches their work environment (e.g., an Artistic person in an Artistic job)
  • Consistency: Some type combinations are more related to each other (adjacent on the hexagon, e.g., RI or SE) than others (opposite, e.g., RA or SC). Consistent profiles are more stable and predictable.
  • Differentiation: A person who strongly resembles one type and little resembles others is well-differentiated. A flat profile (similar scores across all types) is undifferentiated and harder to interpret.
  • Identity: The clarity and stability of a person's goals, interests, and talents
  • Calculus: The hexagonal arrangement reflects the relationships among the types -- adjacent types are most similar; opposite types are most different
EPPP Key Point: The hexagonal model arranges types so that adjacent types (e.g., R-I, I-A, A-S, S-E, E-C, C-R) are most similar, and opposite types (R-S, I-E, A-C) are most dissimilar. Congruence predicts job satisfaction, stability, and achievement.
prev_last_paragraph: Interest inventories are assessment instruments designed to measure an individual's preferences for various activities, occupations, and work environments. They are primarily used in career counseling and vocational guidance. Unlike aptitude or ability tests, interest inventories do not measure what a person can do, but rather what they prefer to do. For the EPPP, you should know the major instruments, their theoretical foundations, and the specific scales and scores they produce.

section_html:
Self-Directed Search (SDS)

The Self-Directed Search was developed by John Holland himself as a self-administered, self-scored, and self-interpreted career exploration tool. It is the most direct operationalization of Holland's RIASEC theory.

Structure

  • The SDS consists of four sections: Activities (liked/disliked), Competencies (can/cannot do), Occupations (appealing/not), and Self-Estimates (self-rated abilities)
  • Each section yields scores for all six RIASEC types
  • The three highest scores form the individual's three-letter Holland code (called the Summary Code)
  • The code is then used with the Occupations Finder or Dictionary of Holland Occupational Codes to identify matching occupations

Strengths and Limitations

  • Strengths: Self-administered and quick (20-30 minutes); cost-effective for group use; strong theoretical foundation; well-validated
  • Limitations: Less detailed than the Strong; self-scoring can lead to errors; relies heavily on self-estimates that may be biased; less useful for individuals with undifferentiated profiles
prev_last_paragraph: These five dimensions round out the Strong profile, giving clinicians a way to discuss not just career direction but the day-to-day work conditions under which a client is most likely to thrive. A client who scores high on Risk Taking and low on Team Orientation, for example, might flourish as an independent entrepreneur far more than in a structured corporate environment — even if both settings technically match her occupational interests.

section_html:
Overview of the MMPI Family

The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory is the most widely used and researched objective personality test in clinical psychology. Originally developed by Hathaway and McKinley in 1943, the instrument has undergone several major revisions. For the EPPP, you must understand the MMPI-2, MMPI-2-RF, and MMPI-3, including their scale structures, construction methods, and interpretation strategies.

Historical Development

  • Original MMPI (1943): Hathaway and McKinley developed the instrument at the University of Minnesota using empirical criterion keying -- items were selected based on their ability to discriminate between clinical groups and normals, not based on item content
  • MMPI-2 (1989): Butcher, Dahlstrom, Graham, Tellegen, and Kaemmer restandardized the instrument with a more representative normative sample (N = 2,600). Item content was updated but the clinical scales were preserved. Uniform T-scores were introduced.
  • MMPI-2-RF (2008): Ben-Porath and Tellegen restructured the instrument using factor analysis, creating 51 scales organized hierarchically. The 10 clinical scales were replaced by Restructured Clinical (RC) scales.
  • MMPI-3 (2020): Ben-Porath and Tellegen further revised the RF, with updated norms, revised items, and modernized content. 335 items, 52 scales.
Empirical Criterion Keying: Items are selected not based on their face validity (what they appear to measure) but based on their empirical ability to discriminate between criterion groups (e.g., patients diagnosed with depression vs. normals). This approach means that an item about headaches might appear on the Depression scale -- not because headaches are theoretically related to depression, but because depressed individuals endorsed that item significantly more often than non-depressed individuals.

MMPI-2: Structure and Scales

The MMPI-2 contains 567 true/false items, takes approximately 60-90 minutes to administer, and requires a sixth-grade reading level. It is normed for ages 18 and older.

Validity Scales

The validity scales assess the test-taking attitude and response style of the examinee. They must be evaluated before interpreting the clinical scales.

ScaleNameWhat It Measures
? (CNS)Cannot SayNumber of items left unanswered. More than 30 unanswered items invalidates the profile.
LLieNaive, unsophisticated attempts to present oneself in a favorable light. Denying common human faults. Elevated L = "faking good" or rigid/moralistic personality.
FInfrequencyItems endorsed by fewer than 10% of the normative sample. Elevated F = "faking bad," exaggeration, random responding, severe psychopathology, or a "cry for help."
KDefensivenessMore sophisticated defensiveness than L. Moderate K = healthy self-presentation; very high K = denial/defensiveness; very low K = excessive openness or self-criticism.
FbBack FInfrequency items from the second half of the test. Detects changes in response style partway through administration.
VRINVariable Response InconsistencyPairs of items with similar or opposite content; inconsistent responding suggests random or careless responding.
TRINTrue Response InconsistencyPairs of items where answering both True or both False is contradictory. Detects acquiescence (yea-saying) or nay-saying bias.
FpInfrequency-PsychopathologyItems infrequently endorsed even by psychiatric inpatients. Helps distinguish genuine severe psychopathology (F elevated, Fp normal) from overreporting (both elevated).
SSuperlative Self-PresentationItems reflecting an extremely positive self-view; supplement to L and K for detecting underreporting.

Research by Siegel and Langford (1998) provided empirical support for the association between parental alienation behaviors and defensive responding on the MMPI-2 in custody contexts. Their study compared mothers who demonstrated alienating behaviors — such as persistently disparaging the other parent, interfering with visitation, and attempting to erode the child's bond with the other parent — against mothers who did not exhibit these patterns. The alienating mothers produced statistically significant elevations on both the L and K validity scales relative to the comparison group, while simultaneously obtaining significantly lower F scale scores. This triad of findings indicates that mothers engaging in alienation were substantially more invested in portraying themselves as free of psychological difficulties and as morally upstanding. The suppressed F scores further suggest active denial of even minor imperfections or common human frailties. This research underscores the importance of carefully scrutinizing validity scale configurations in forensic assessments, as individuals motivated to gain legal advantage may produce profiles that systematically underrepresent genuine psychological characteristics.

Example

A mother undergoing a custody evaluation produces an L scale T-score of 72, a K scale T-score of 68, and an F scale T-score of 42. Her clinical scales are uniformly within normal limits. Drawing on Siegel and Langford's findings, the evaluator would consider the possibility that this highly defensive profile may be masking clinically relevant characteristics. The evaluator should examine collateral evidence — such as court records, teacher reports, and the child's statements — to determine whether alienating behaviors are present and whether the suppressed clinical profile reflects genuine adjustment or impression management.

EPPP Commonly Tested: F-K Index (Gough Dissimulation Index): F minus K. A positive value (F > K) suggests overreporting/faking bad. A negative value (K > F) suggests underreporting/faking good. This index is commonly tested.

Validity scale patterns carry particular significance in forensic settings, especially child custody evaluations. Parents engaged in custody disputes frequently present themselves in an overly favorable manner, but research has identified distinctive profiles among specific subgroups. Parents who display behaviors consistent with parental alienation syndrome — characterized by systematic denigration of the other parent and efforts to undermine the child's relationship with that parent — tend to produce a characteristic defensive pattern on the MMPI-2. Specifically, these individuals typically obtain elevated scores on the L (Lie) and K (Defensiveness) scales, reflecting a strong motivation to appear psychologically healthy and morally virtuous. Simultaneously, their F (Infrequency) scale scores tend to fall below average, indicating a deliberate minimization of any psychological symptoms or personal shortcomings. This L↑ K↑ F↓ configuration represents a classic underreporting profile and should alert the clinician to the possibility that the individual is managing their self-presentation in a highly controlled manner, which may limit the interpretability of the clinical scales.

Clinical Note

In custody evaluations, a defensive validity profile (high L and K, low F) does not automatically indicate parental alienation or dishonesty — many custody litigants produce similar profiles due to the high-stakes nature of the evaluation. The clinician must integrate MMPI-2 findings with interview data, collateral reports, behavioral observations, and the specific referral questions before drawing conclusions about alienating behavior.

Clinical Scales

ScaleNameAbbreviationElevated Score Interpretation
1HypochondriasisHsExcessive somatic concern, vague physical complaints, pessimism, demanding
2DepressionDDepressed mood, psychomotor retardation, hopelessness, social withdrawal
3HysteriaHySomatic complaints with denial of psychological problems, need for attention, naive/superficial
4Psychopathic DeviatePdAntisocial behavior, rebelliousness, family conflict, impulsivity, authority problems
5Masculinity-FemininityMfInterests differing from traditional gender roles; interpretation depends on gender and context
6ParanoiaPaSuspiciousness, sensitivity, hostility, rigidity, paranoid ideation, persecutory beliefs
7PsychastheniaPtAnxiety, obsessive-compulsive features, guilt, self-doubt, indecisiveness, rumination
8SchizophreniaScBizarre thinking, social alienation, unusual perceptions, poor reality testing, confusion
9HypomaniaMaElevated mood, grandiosity, hyperactivity, impulsivity, flight of ideas, irritability
0Social IntroversionSiSocial withdrawal, shyness, discomfort in social situations; low scores = extroversion

T-Score Interpretation

  • Clinical scales use Uniform T-scores (developed by Auke Tellegen) to ensure comparable percentile rankings across scales
  • T-score of 65 or above is considered clinically significant (93rd percentile)
  • T-scores between 60-64 are marginally elevated
  • Scales 5 (Mf) and 0 (Si) use linear T-scores rather than uniform T-scores because their distributions are close to normal

Originally developed by Hathaway and McKinley in 1943, the instrument has undergone several major revisions. section_html:
MMPI-2-RF (Restructured Form)

The MMPI-2-RF (Ben-Porath & Tellegen, 2008) contains 338 items and uses a hierarchically organized structure of 51 scales. The key innovation was removing the demoralization variance (a general distress factor) that permeated and inflated correlations among the original clinical scales.

Scale Hierarchy

  1. Validity Scales (9): CNS, VRIN-r, TRIN-r, F-r, Fp-r, Fs, FBS-r, L-r, K-r
  2. Higher-Order (H-O) Scales (3): Emotional/Internalizing Dysfunction (EID), Thought Dysfunction (THD), Behavioral/Externalizing Dysfunction (BXD)
  3. Restructured Clinical (RC) Scales (9): The core interpretive scales
    • RCd: Demoralization (general unhappiness/distress)
    • RC1: Somatic Complaints
    • RC2: Low Positive Emotions
    • RC3: Cynicism
    • RC4: Antisocial Behavior
    • RC6: Ideas of Persecution
    • RC7: Dysfunctional Negative Emotions
    • RC8: Aberrant Experiences
    • RC9: Hypomanic Activation
  4. Specific Problems (SP) Scales (23): Provide detailed information within domains (e.g., Head Pain Complaints, Stress/Worry, Juvenile Conduct Problems)
  5. Interest Scales (2): Aesthetic-Literary Interests, Mechanical-Physical Interests
  6. Personality Psychopathology Five (PSY-5) Scales (5): Aggressiveness-Revised, Psychoticism-Revised, Disconstraint-Revised, Negative Emotionality/Neuroticism-Revised, Introversion/Low Positive Emotionality-Revised
Key Distinction: The MMPI-2-RF RC scales differ from the original clinical scales primarily in the removal of the demoralization factor. In the original MMPI-2, many clinical scales intercorrelated highly because they all contained items tapping general distress. The RC scales isolate the distinctive core construct of each scale, improving discriminant validity.
prev_last_paragraph: The Harris-Lingoes subscales, developed by Harris and Lingoes in 1955, address exactly this problem. They break the heterogeneous clinical scales into more homogeneous content clusters, allowing clinicians to pinpoint the specific themes underlying an elevation. For example, if Scale 4 is elevated, the Harris-Lingoes subscales can reveal whether the elevation stems primarily from Family Discord (Pd1), Authority Problems (Pd2), Social Imperturbability (Pd3), Social Alienation (Pd4), or Self-Alienation (Pd5). These subscales exist for Scales 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 9 — notably, scales that are especially content-diverse. Clinicians find them particularly valuable when refining diagnostic hypotheses and when two clients share an identical code type yet present with very different clinical pictures.

section_html:
MMPI-3

The MMPI-3 (Ben-Porath & Tellegen, 2020) is the latest version, containing 335 items and 52 scales. It retains the hierarchical structure of the MMPI-2-RF with several key updates:

  • Updated normative sample (N = 1,620) that is more representative of the U.S. population
  • Revised and modernized item content (removed outdated or offensive items)
  • New scales addressing interpersonal functioning and compulsive behaviors
  • Improved validity scales for detecting over- and underreporting
  • Updated PSY-5 scales

Key Differences from MMPI-2-RF

  • The MMPI-3 replaces some specific problems scales and adds new ones (e.g., Compulsivity, Self-Importance)
  • The normative sample is more diverse and contemporary
  • Item content was further refined for clarity and modern language
  • The MMPI-3 is not backward-compatible with the MMPI-2 or MMPI-2-RF
prev_last_paragraph: The MMPI-2-RF (Ben-Porath & Tellegen, 2008) contains 338 items and uses a hierarchically organized structure of 51 scales. The key innovation was removing the demoralization variance (a general distress factor) that permeated and inflated correlations among the original clinical scales.

section_html:
Overview of Personality Measures

This chapter covers personality assessment instruments beyond the MMPI family. These include objective (self-report) personality inventories and projective (performance-based) techniques. For the EPPP, you must know the theoretical basis, structure, scoring, and appropriate uses of each major instrument, as well as the ongoing debate about the reliability and validity of projective methods.

Objective vs. Projective: Objective personality tests use structured, standardized items (typically true/false or Likert-scale) with empirically derived scoring. Projective tests present ambiguous stimuli and assume that responses reveal underlying personality dynamics, unconscious conflicts, and thought organization. Modern terminology increasingly refers to projective tests as "performance-based" measures to reduce theoretical assumptions embedded in the name.

T-Scores

A T-score is a standardized score with M = 50 and SD = 10. T-scores eliminate the negative numbers and decimals of z-scores, making them easier to communicate.

Formula: T = 10(z) + 50, or equivalently, T = 10[(X - M) / SD] + 50. A T-score of 50 = the mean. A T-score of 60 = 1 SD above the mean. A T-score of 30 = 2 SDs below the mean.

A common EPPP item tests whether examinees can identify score boundaries within the normal distribution. Since approximately 99.7% of all scores fall within ±3 standard deviations of the mean, a T-score of 20 (which corresponds to z = -3.0) effectively represents the floor of obtainable scores in a normally distributed population. However, when the question frame restricts the range to ±1 standard deviation — where roughly 68% of all examinees score — then a T-score of 40 (z = -1.0) marks the lowest score within that central band. Recognizing which reference frame a question uses is critical: "lowest score in the distribution" points to T = 20, whereas "lowest score within one SD of the mean" points to T = 40. On the EPPP, reading whether the stem specifies the full distribution or only the middle 68% determines the correct answer.

When evaluating clinical significance on instruments that use T-scores, the value of 65 warrants special attention. On the MMPI-2 clinical scales, a T-score of 65 is the threshold for clinical elevation — it falls 1.5 standard deviations above the mean and corresponds to approximately the 93rd–95th percentile in the normative sample. Among the fixed response options typically offered on EPPP items asking which T-score represents "the highest" or most clinically significant result, T = 65 is frequently the correct answer because higher T-scores on pathology-oriented measures indicate greater deviation from the normative mean. A T-score of 65 surpasses the more moderate values of 40 (one SD below the mean), 50 (the mean itself), or 60 (one SD above). Recognizing that T = 65 marks the clinical cutoff on the MMPI-2 — and represents the most extreme score when compared against common alternatives — is essential for accurate EPPP performance.

Common Uses

  • MMPI-2, MMPI-2-RF, MMPI-3: All scales reported as T-scores (clinical significance at T >= 65)
  • NEO-PI-R: Domain and facet scores reported as T-scores
  • Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF): T-scores with clinical cutoff at 65
  • Many behavioral checklists and symptom measures use T-scores

Linear vs. Normalized T-Scores

  • Linear T-scores: Direct transformation of raw scores (preserves original distribution shape). Used on MMPI-2 Scales 5 and 0.
  • Normalized T-scores: Raw scores are first transformed to percentile ranks, then converted to T-scores based on the normal distribution. This forces the distribution into a normal shape.
  • Uniform T-scores: Used on most MMPI-2 clinical scales. A method developed by Tellegen that ensures the percentile value of a given T-score is the same across all scales, even though the raw score distributions differ.
prev_last_paragraph: The z-score is the most fundamental derived score. It expresses how many standard deviations a raw score falls above or below the mean of its distribution.

section_html:

Standard scores with M = 100 and SD = 15 are used by the Wechsler scales, Stanford-Binet 5, and most other intelligence and cognitive ability tests for composite/index scores.

Stanines

Stanines (standard nines) divide the normal distribution into 9 units with M = 5 and SD = approximately 2. Each stanine (except 1 and 9) spans a half standard deviation.
