prev_last_paragraph: Consider a normally distributed set of 1,000 test scores. Most raw scores cluster near the mean, with fewer scores at the extremes. After converting to percentile ranks, however, exactly 100 examinees occupy each 10-percentile band (1–10, 11–20, … 91–100). The original bell-shaped concentration near the center has been spread evenly across the full percentile range, yielding a flat, rectangular distribution.

section_html:
Normal Curve Equivalents (NCEs)

Normal Curve Equivalents are standard scores with M = 50 and SD = 21.06. They were developed for use in federally funded educational programs (e.g., Title I evaluations) to allow averaging and statistical comparison of scores across different tests.

  • Range: 1 to 99
  • NCEs of 1, 50, and 99 correspond to percentile ranks of 1, 50, and 99
  • Unlike percentile ranks, NCEs are on an equal-interval scale and can be meaningfully averaged
  • NCEs are rarely used in clinical practice but may appear on the EPPP
prev_last_paragraph: Stanines are commonly used in educational testing and provide a coarse but useful classification. The percentages 4-7-12-17-20-17-12-7-4 should be memorized.

section_html:
Standard Error of Measurement (SEM)

The Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) quantifies the amount of error in an individual's observed test score. It reflects the fact that no test is perfectly reliable -- an individual's observed score may differ from their "true score" due to measurement error.

Formula: SEM = SD * sqrt(1 - rxx), where SD = standard deviation of the test scores and rxx = reliability coefficient of the test. Higher reliability yields a smaller SEM (less measurement error). A perfectly reliable test (r = 1.0) would have SEM = 0.

SEM Properties

  • The SEM is in the same units as the test score
  • The SEM decreases as reliability increases
  • The SEM is assumed to be constant across all score levels (though in practice, it may vary)
  • The SEM is used to construct confidence intervals around an observed score
Example: A test has SD = 15 and reliability = .91. SEM = 15 * sqrt(1 - .91) = 15 * sqrt(.09) = 15 * 0.30 = 4.5. For the WAIS-IV FSIQ (reliability ~.98), SEM ~ 15 * sqrt(.02) ~ 2.1 points. This means the FSIQ is measured with very high precision.
prev_last_paragraph: Normal Curve Equivalents are standard scores with M = 50 and SD = 21.06. They were developed for use in federally funded educational programs (e.g., Title I evaluations) to allow averaging and statistical comparison of scores across different tests.

section_html:
Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval (CI) provides a range around the observed score within which the true score is likely to fall, given a specified level of confidence.

Banding in Personnel Selection

Banding is a score interpretation strategy used in employment testing that treats scores within a specified range as functionally equivalent. The underlying rationale is that minor differences in test scores do not reliably correspond to meaningful differences in actual job performance. Because all test scores contain measurement error, two candidates whose scores differ by less than the standard error of the difference may not truly differ in the construct being measured. Banding uses the SEM and confidence intervals to define a band of scores that are statistically indistinguishable from one another.

In practice, banding allows employers to select from among candidates within the same score band using secondary criteria (e.g., diversity goals, relevant experience, organizational fit) rather than rigidly rank-ordering applicants by fractions of a point. The width of the band is typically determined by computing the standard error of the difference between scores; candidates whose scores fall within this range are considered to have performed equivalently on the selection instrument.

There are two primary approaches to banding:

Type Description Characteristics
Fixed Bands Predetermined score ranges that remain constant throughout the selection process Simpler to administer; all candidates within a band are treated as equivalent before moving to the next band
Sliding Bands The band "slides" downward as the highest-scoring candidate within the current band is selected More flexible; the band is recalculated after each selection decision, potentially including lower-scoring candidates as top scorers are hired

Clinical Note

Banding has been the subject of legal and professional debate. Proponents argue it appropriately acknowledges measurement imprecision and can promote workforce diversity without sacrificing validity. Critics contend that sliding bands may deviate from strict merit-based selection. The EPPP may test your understanding that banding is grounded in the psychometric principle that observed score differences smaller than measurement error should not be treated as reflecting genuine ability differences.

Construction

  • 68% CI: Observed score +/- 1 SEM
  • 90% CI: Observed score +/- 1.645 SEM
  • 95% CI: Observed score +/- 1.96 SEM (often rounded to 2 SEM)
  • 99% CI: Observed score +/- 2.576 SEM
Example: An examinee obtains an IQ of 112 on a test with SEM = 4.5. The 95% CI = 112 +/- (1.96 x 4.5) = 112 +/- 8.82, or approximately 103 to 121. We can state with 95% confidence that the individual's true IQ falls between 103 and 121.
EPPP Practice Point: Reporting confidence intervals rather than single scores is considered best practice because it communicates the inherent imprecision in any test score. APA guidelines recommend that psychologists report confidence intervals when communicating test results.
prev_last_paragraph: The Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) quantifies the amount of error in an individual's observed test score. It reflects the fact that no test is perfectly reliable -- an individual's observed score may differ from their "true score" due to measurement error.

section_html:
Regression to the Mean

Regression to the mean is the statistical phenomenon whereby extreme scores on a first measurement tend to be less extreme on subsequent measurements. This occurs because any observed score contains both true score variance and error variance, and the error component is random.

Key Implications

  • A student who scores very high on a test is likely to score somewhat lower on retest (and vice versa) -- not because their ability changed, but because the extreme score was partly due to random error in the favorable direction
  • Regression to the mean is more pronounced when reliability is lower (more error variance) and when the initial score is more extreme
  • This effect must be considered when evaluating treatment outcomes: improvement from an extremely low baseline may partly reflect regression to the mean rather than true treatment effects
  • The estimated true score = M + rxx(X - M), where M = population mean, rxx = reliability, and X = observed score. This formula shows that the estimated true score is always closer to the mean than the observed score (regressed toward the mean by a factor of the reliability coefficient)
Estimated True Score Formula: Estimated True Score = M + r(X - M). If a test has M = 100, r = .90, and an individual scores 130, the estimated true score = 100 + .90(130 - 100) = 100 + 27 = 127. The estimated true score (127) is regressed 3 points toward the mean from the observed score (130).
EPPP Application: When predicting retest scores, always expect regression to the mean. An individual who scored 75 (low) is predicted to score somewhat higher on retest; an individual who scored 130 (high) is predicted to score somewhat lower. The amount of regression depends on the test's reliability -- lower reliability produces more regression.
prev_last_paragraph: The Reliable Change Index (RCI) (Jacobson & Truax, 1991) determines whether the difference between two test scores (e.g., pre- and post-treatment) reflects true change rather than measurement error.

section_html:
Overview of the Wechsler Scales

The Wechsler intelligence scales are the most widely used individually administered intelligence tests in the world. Developed by David Wechsler beginning in 1939, the scales are based on Wechsler's definition of intelligence as "the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with his environment." The current editions include measures for adults, children, and preschoolers.

Wechsler's Definition: Intelligence is not a single ability but an aggregate of abilities. Wechsler also emphasized that non-intellective factors (motivation, persistence, emotional regulation) influence intelligent behavior. This holistic view influenced his decision to include both verbal and performance measures.
next_heading_text: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale - Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV)

section_html:
IQ Classification System

The WAIS-IV, WISC-V, and SB5 all use M = 100, SD = 15. The following classification system is commonly used:

IQ RangeClassificationPercentile RangePrevalence
130+Very Superior / Extremely High98th+~2.2%
120-129Superior / Very High91st-97th~6.7%
110-119High Average75th-90th~16.1%
90-109Average25th-74th~50%
80-89Low Average9th-24th~16.1%
70-79Borderline2nd-8th~6.7%
69 and belowExtremely Low / Intellectual Disability rangeBelow 2nd~2.2%
EPPP Note: A diagnosis of intellectual disability requires: (1) significantly subaverage intellectual functioning (typically IQ ~70 or below), (2) concurrent deficits in adaptive functioning, and (3) onset during the developmental period (before age 18). An IQ score alone is never sufficient for the diagnosis.
prev_last_paragraph: The SB5's routing procedure directly addresses floor and ceiling concerns by tailoring item difficulty to each examinee's functional level. Because examinees begin subsequent subtests at a difficulty level matched to their performance on the routing subtests, very low-ability individuals receive easier item sets that can capture fine-grained differences among them, while very high-ability individuals encounter sufficiently challenging items. The SB5's extended IQ range of 40 to 160 further mitigates these effects compared to instruments with narrower score ranges. This makes the SB5 especially well-suited for evaluating individuals at extreme ends of the distribution, such as those being assessed for intellectual giftedness or intellectual disability.

section_html:
Factor Structure and CHC Theory

Modern intelligence tests are organized around the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory, which integrates Cattell and Horn's Gf-Gc theory with Carroll's three-stratum model:

  • Stratum III: General intelligence (g)
  • Stratum II: Broad abilities -- Gf (Fluid Reasoning), Gc (Crystallized Ability), Gv (Visual Processing), Gsm (Short-Term Memory), Gs (Processing Speed), Glr (Long-Term Retrieval), Ga (Auditory Processing), Gq (Quantitative Knowledge), and others
  • Stratum I: Narrow abilities (specific skills measured by individual subtests)

Gf vs. Gc

Research on cognitive training has revealed a notable relationship between working memory training and fluid intelligence. Studies, most notably by Jaeggi and colleagues (2008), demonstrated that when adults practiced intensive working memory tasks (such as the dual n-back paradigm) over multiple sessions, they showed measurable gains on fluid intelligence assessments — even when those Gf measures were structurally dissimilar to the training exercises. This finding was significant because it challenged the longstanding assumption that fluid reasoning capacity was essentially fixed and resistant to environmental intervention.

The theoretical explanation centers on the substantial cognitive overlap between working memory and fluid reasoning. Both abilities require maintaining and manipulating information in real time, inhibiting irrelevant stimuli, and managing attentional resources. By strengthening the executive control processes underlying working memory, training appears to produce transfer effects that generalize to novel problem-solving tasks characteristic of Gf measurement. The gains tended to be dose-dependent, with longer training periods producing larger improvements.

Clinical Note

While initial findings generated considerable enthusiasm, subsequent meta-analyses have produced mixed results regarding the durability and magnitude of far-transfer effects from working memory training to fluid intelligence. Clinicians should be cautious about overstating the benefits of commercial "brain training" programs. The evidence is strongest for structured, adaptive working memory interventions delivered over sustained periods, and even then, the extent to which gains persist after training cessation remains debated.

  • Fluid Intelligence (Gf): The ability to reason, solve novel problems, and identify patterns without relying on previously acquired knowledge. Largely biologically determined. Peaks in young adulthood and declines with age.
  • Crystallized Intelligence (Gc): Accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, and skills acquired through education and experience. Largely culturally and educationally influenced. Continues to grow throughout the lifespan (or at least remains stable into late life).
Aging Pattern: Gf declines with age (particularly after age 60-70), while Gc remains stable or increases through middle and later adulthood. This produces the "classic aging pattern" on the Wechsler scales: relatively preserved VCI with declining PSI and WMI scores. Processing speed (Gs) shows the earliest and most pronounced age-related decline.
prev_last_paragraph: Think of it this way: imagine you measured your height against a doorframe in 1997 and marked it at a certain point. If someone later replaced that doorframe with a taller one, your mark would appear lower — not because you shrank, but because the reference point changed. The Flynn Effect operates similarly. Clinicians must always check whether the test edition they are using — or interpreting results from — has current, appropriate norms, and they should be prepared to discuss the Flynn Effect whenever historical IQ scores are being used in high-stakes decisions.

heading_text: Overview of Standard 5: Advertising and Other Public Statements
section_html:
Overview of Standard 5: Advertising and Other Public Statements

Standard 5 (Advertising and Other Public Statements) of the APA Ethics Code addresses truthfulness in professional representations. Psychologists have an obligation to ensure that all public statements about their services, qualifications, and research are accurate, not deceptive, and do not mislead the public.

This standard is tested on the EPPP because violations in advertising can directly harm the public and undermine trust in the profession.
next_heading_text: Standard 5: Advertising and Other Public Statements

section_html:
Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)

SSRIs are the most commonly prescribed class of antidepressants and are generally considered first-line treatment for depression and many anxiety disorders due to their relatively favorable side effect profile.

Mechanism of Action

SSRIs selectively block the reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) at the presynaptic neuron, increasing the availability of serotonin in the synaptic cleft. They have minimal effects on norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake.

Common SSRIs

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
FluoxetineProzacLongest half-life (~2-6 days; active metabolite norfluoxetine ~4-16 days); approved for children/adolescents with depression; less risk of discontinuation syndrome
SertralineZoloftMild dopamine reuptake inhibition; commonly prescribed for PTSD; considered safe in cardiac patients
ParoxetinePaxilMost anticholinergic of the SSRIs; short half-life leading to higher discontinuation risk; associated with weight gain; NOT recommended in pregnancy (Category D)
CitalopramCelexaMost selective SSRI; dose-dependent QT prolongation risk; FDA max dose 40 mg/day
EscitalopramLexaproS-enantiomer of citalopram; may have fewer drug interactions; commonly used for generalized anxiety disorder
FluvoxamineLuvoxPrimarily used for OCD; significant drug-drug interactions via CYP enzymes

Common Side Effects of SSRIs

  • Sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, anorgasmia, erectile dysfunction) -- most common reason for discontinuation
  • Gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, diarrhea)
  • Headache, insomnia, or drowsiness
  • Weight gain (especially paroxetine) or weight loss
  • Increased anxiety initially (may worsen before improving)
  • Discontinuation syndrome with abrupt cessation (dizziness, nausea, "brain zaps," irritability)
prev_last_paragraph: Antidepressants generally take 2-6 weeks to reach full therapeutic effect, although side effects may begin immediately. This delay is thought to relate to downstream neuroplastic changes rather than the acute increase in neurotransmitter availability.

section_html:
Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs)

SNRIs block the reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine, providing a dual mechanism that may be beneficial for patients who do not respond to SSRIs alone. They are also used for chronic pain conditions, fibromyalgia, and neuropathic pain.

Common SNRIs

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
VenlafaxineEffexorAt low doses, primarily serotonergic; norepinephrine effects emerge at higher doses; may increase blood pressure; significant discontinuation syndrome
DuloxetineCymbaltaFDA-approved for MDD, GAD, fibromyalgia, diabetic neuropathic pain, and chronic musculoskeletal pain; hepatotoxicity risk (avoid in liver disease)
DesvenlafaxinePristiqActive metabolite of venlafaxine; fewer drug interactions; simpler dosing
LevomilnacipranFetzimaGreater selectivity for norepinephrine than serotonin; may be more activating

Side Effects of SNRIs

  • Similar to SSRIs (sexual dysfunction, nausea, headache)
  • Elevated blood pressure (especially venlafaxine at higher doses) -- blood pressure monitoring recommended
  • Increased sweating
  • Discontinuation syndrome (particularly severe with venlafaxine due to its short half-life)
prev_last_paragraph: SSRIs selectively block the reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) at the presynaptic neuron, increasing the availability of serotonin in the synaptic cleft. They have minimal effects on norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake.

section_html:
Atypical Antidepressants

Several antidepressants do not fit neatly into the above categories and are classified as atypical antidepressants.

Esketamine (Spravato)

Esketamine represents a significant advancement in the treatment of depression that has not responded to adequate trials of conventional antidepressants. Approved by the FDA in 2019, esketamine is the S-enantiomer of ketamine, an NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptor antagonist. Unlike traditional antidepressants that target monoamine systems and require weeks to take effect, esketamine acts on the glutamatergic system and can produce rapid antidepressant effects — often within hours to days. It is administered as a nasal spray and is specifically indicated for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), defined as depression that has failed to respond to at least two adequate antidepressant trials in the current episode.

Because of concerns about dissociative effects, sedation, abuse potential, and transient increases in blood pressure, esketamine is available only through a restricted distribution system called the REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) program. Patients must be observed in a certified healthcare setting for at least two hours following each administration. The medication is used as an adjunct to an oral antidepressant rather than as monotherapy. Common adverse effects include dissociation, dizziness, nausea, sedation, vertigo, and a feeling of disconnection from reality. These effects are typically transient and resolve within the monitoring period.

Clinical Note

Esketamine's rapid onset of action makes it a particularly valuable option for patients in acute depressive crises, including those with suicidal ideation. In 2020, the FDA expanded its approval to include depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder accompanied by acute suicidal thinking or behavior. Psychologists should be aware that patients receiving esketamine may experience perceptual disturbances and should not drive or operate machinery until the following day after a restful sleep.

Bupropion (Wellbutrin)

  • Mechanism: Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI); does NOT affect serotonin
  • Uses: Depression, smoking cessation (marketed as Zyban), ADHD (off-label)
  • Advantages: No sexual dysfunction (may actually improve libido); no weight gain (may cause weight loss); activating rather than sedating
  • Risks: Lowers seizure threshold (contraindicated in patients with seizure disorders, eating disorders, or those undergoing abrupt alcohol withdrawal); may increase anxiety

Mirtazapine (Remeron)

  • Mechanism: Noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA); blocks alpha-2 autoreceptors (increasing NE and 5-HT release) and 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors; potent H1 antagonist
  • Uses: Depression, especially with insomnia, poor appetite, or weight loss
  • Side effects: Significant sedation and weight gain (due to H1 blockade); increased appetite; useful when these "side effects" are actually therapeutic goals
  • Advantages: Minimal sexual dysfunction; helpful for nausea (5-HT3 blockade)

Trazodone (Desyrel)

  • Mechanism: Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI)
  • Uses: Primarily used as a sleep aid at low doses; antidepressant at higher doses (rarely used this way due to sedation)
  • Side effects: Sedation, orthostatic hypotension, priapism (rare but serious -- prolonged painful erection requiring emergency treatment)
prev_last_paragraph: MAOIs have dangerous interactions with many medications, including SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, meperidine (Demerol), dextromethorphan, and sympathomimetic drugs. A washout period of at least 2 weeks is required when switching between MAOIs and serotonergic medications (5 weeks for fluoxetine due to its long half-life).

section_html:
The FDA Black Box Warning

In 2004, the FDA issued a black box warning -- the strongest warning the FDA can require -- for all antidepressants regarding the increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (up to age 24) during the initial weeks of treatment.

  • The warning applies to all antidepressants, not just SSRIs
  • The risk appears to be highest during the first 1-2 months of treatment or after dose changes
  • The mechanism is thought to involve an initial increase in energy and motivation before mood fully improves, potentially enabling a suicidal individual to act on preexisting ideation
  • Close monitoring is recommended during the initial period of treatment, especially in young patients
  • The warning does NOT state that antidepressants should not be prescribed to young people; the benefits generally outweigh the risks, but careful monitoring is essential
EPPP Tip

The black box warning is limited to ages 24 and under. For adults aged 25-64, antidepressants showed no increased suicidality, and for adults 65+, antidepressants appeared to reduce suicidal risk. The only SSRI FDA-approved for use in children with depression is fluoxetine (ages 8+).
prev_last_paragraph: Treatment: Discontinue all serotonergic agents; supportive care; cyproheptadine (a serotonin antagonist) may be used in severe cases; benzodiazepines for agitation.

section_html:
The Dopamine Hypothesis of Schizophrenia

The dopamine hypothesis proposes that schizophrenia symptoms result from dysregulated dopamine activity in the brain:

  • Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought) are associated with excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway
  • Negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia) are associated with reduced dopamine activity in the mesocortical pathway (prefrontal cortex)

This helps explain why typical antipsychotics, which broadly block dopamine D2 receptors, effectively treat positive symptoms but often worsen negative symptoms and cause movement disorders (due to dopamine blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway).

Four Dopamine Pathways

Mesolimbic: Excess dopamine leads to positive symptoms. Mesocortical: Reduced dopamine leads to negative and cognitive symptoms. Nigrostriatal: Dopamine blockade here causes EPS and tardive dyskinesia. Tuberoinfundibular: Dopamine blockade here increases prolactin, causing hyperprolactinemia.
prev_last_paragraph: ExampleA patient with comorbid major depression and diabetic neuropathy may benefit from duloxetine because it addresses both the mood disorder and the chronic pain condition through a single medication, reducing polypharmacy burden.

section_html:
First-Generation (Typical) Antipsychotics

First-generation antipsychotics (FGAs) work primarily by blocking dopamine D2 receptors. They are classified by potency, which determines their side effect profile.

High-Potency Typical Antipsychotics

Require lower doses; greater risk of EPS; lower risk of sedation and anticholinergic effects.

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
HaloperidolHaldolMost commonly used high-potency typical; available in decanoate (long-acting injectable) form; high EPS risk
FluphenazineProlixinAlso available as long-acting decanoate; high EPS risk
ThiothixeneNavaneHigh potency; primarily D2 blockade
PimozideOrapFDA-approved for Tourette's disorder; QT prolongation risk

Low-Potency Typical Antipsychotics

Require higher doses; lower risk of EPS; greater sedation, anticholinergic effects, and orthostatic hypotension.

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
ChlorpromazineThorazineFirst antipsychotic discovered (1950s); highly sedating; photosensitivity; corneal deposits with chronic use; "benchmark" drug (100 mg = standard unit for potency comparisons)
ThioridazineMellarilHighest risk of retinitis pigmentosa; QT prolongation; restricted use due to cardiac risks
prev_last_paragraph: Mesolimbic: Excess dopamine leads to positive symptoms. Mesocortical: Reduced dopamine leads to negative and cognitive symptoms. Nigrostriatal: Dopamine blockade here causes EPS and tardive dyskinesia. Tuberoinfundibular: Dopamine blockade here increases prolactin, causing hyperprolactinemia.

section_html:
Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS)

Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) are movement disorders caused by dopamine D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway. They are most common with high-potency typical antipsychotics.

EPS TypeOnsetFeaturesTreatment
Acute dystoniaHours to daysSustained muscle contractions (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonus); can be life-threatening if laryngeal muscles affectedAnticholinergics (benztropine/Cogentin, diphenhydramine/Benadryl)
AkathisiaDays to weeksSubjective restlessness; inability to sit still; often mistaken for agitationBeta-blockers (propranolol), benzodiazepines, dose reduction
Parkinsonism (pseudoparkinsonism)Weeks to monthsBradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, mask-like faciesAnticholinergics (benztropine); amantadine; dose reduction
Tardive dyskinesiaMonths to yearsInvoluntary, repetitive movements (especially orofacial: lip smacking, tongue protrusion, chewing, grimacing); may be irreversibleDiscontinue or reduce offending agent if possible; valbenazine (Ingrezza) or deutetrabenazine (Austedo) -- VMAT2 inhibitors approved for TD
EPPP Tip

Know the timeline: acute dystonia appears within hours to days, akathisia within days to weeks, parkinsonism within weeks to months, and tardive dyskinesia after months to years of use. TD is the most feared because it may be irreversible and paradoxically may worsen when the offending drug is discontinued.
prev_last_paragraph: Require higher doses; lower risk of EPS; greater sedation, anticholinergic effects, and orthostatic hypotension.

section_html:
Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics

Atypical antipsychotics block both dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This dual mechanism, known as serotonin-dopamine antagonism (SDA), is thought to reduce EPS risk and improve negative symptoms compared to typical antipsychotics.

Common Atypical Antipsychotics

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
ClozapineClozarilGold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; lowest EPS risk; most effective for refractory positive and negative symptoms; also reduces suicidality in schizophrenia. SERIOUS RISK: agranulocytosis (1-2%) requiring mandatory blood monitoring (weekly for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly)
RisperidoneRisperdalHigher EPS risk than other atypicals at higher doses (dose-dependent D2 blockade); significant prolactin elevation; available as long-acting injectable (Risperdal Consta)
OlanzapineZyprexaHighest risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome; structurally similar to clozapine; effective but metabolic concerns limit use
QuetiapineSeroquelVery sedating at lower doses; used off-label for insomnia and anxiety; lower EPS risk; less prolactin elevation
ZiprasidoneGeodonWeight-neutral; lowest metabolic risk among atypicals; QT prolongation concern; should be taken with food for absorption
AripiprazoleAbilifyPartial dopamine agonist (D2 partial agonist); stabilizes dopamine activity; low EPS, low metabolic risk, low sedation; may cause akathisia
LurasidoneLatudaMust be taken with food (350+ calories); lower metabolic risk; approved for bipolar depression
EPPP Tip

Key facts to know: Clozapine = treatment-resistant schizophrenia + agranulocytosis risk + mandatory blood monitoring. Olanzapine = worst metabolic side effects. Aripiprazole = unique partial D2 agonist mechanism. Risperidone = highest prolactin elevation among atypicals.
prev_last_paragraph: Both involve hyperthermia and altered mental status, but NMS features lead-pipe rigidity and develops over days, while serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia, clonus, and myoclonus and develops within hours. NMS is caused by dopamine blockade; serotonin syndrome by serotonin excess. This distinction is a classic exam question. A helpful way to remember: NMS is "slow and stiff" (developing over days with rigid muscles), while serotonin syndrome is "fast and twitchy" (developing within hours with jerky, hyperactive reflexes). Also consider the medication history — NMS follows antipsychotic use, while serotonin syndrome typically follows the initiation or dose increase of serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs) or the combination of multiple serotonergic agents.

section_html:
Metabolic Syndrome

Second-generation antipsychotics (especially clozapine and olanzapine) carry significant risk of metabolic syndrome, which includes:

  • Weight gain (often 10-30+ pounds)
  • Dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides, decreased HDL)
  • Hyperglycemia / Type 2 diabetes
  • Hypertension

Metabolic monitoring (fasting glucose, lipid panel, weight, waist circumference, blood pressure) is recommended at baseline and at regular intervals for all patients on atypical antipsychotics.

Metabolic Risk by Medication (High to Low)

  1. Clozapine and Olanzapine (highest risk)
  2. Quetiapine and Risperidone (moderate risk)
  3. Aripiprazole, Ziprasidone, and Lurasidone (lowest risk)
prev_last_paragraph: While agranulocytosis is most closely associated with clozapine, it is important to recognize the broader category of neutropenia — a reduction in neutrophil count that compromises the body's ability to fight bacterial infections. Agranulocytosis represents the most severe end of this spectrum, defined by an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below 500 cells/μL, which places the patient at critical risk for life-threatening infections. With clozapine, the incidence of agranulocytosis is approximately 1–2%, with the highest risk occurring during the first six months of treatment. Other second-generation antipsychotics (e.g., olanzapine, quetiapine) have been associated with neutropenia on rare occasions, though at rates far lower than clozapine. The mandatory blood monitoring program for clozapine — known as the Clozapine REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) — requires regular ANC checks: weekly for the first six months, biweekly for the next six months, and monthly thereafter if counts remain stable. Treatment must be immediately discontinued if ANC falls below specified thresholds. This monitoring requirement is a defining feature of clozapine management and a frequently tested concept.

section_html:
Overview

This chapter covers anxiolytics (medications used to treat anxiety disorders), including benzodiazepines and buspirone, as well as anti-dementia medications. These medication classes appear regularly on the EPPP because understanding their mechanisms, side effects, and clinical considerations is essential for psychologists collaborating with prescribers.

Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines are the most commonly prescribed anxiolytics. They enhance the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) by binding to the GABA-A receptor complex and increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, leading to neuronal inhibition.

Common Benzodiazepines

Generic NameBrand NameDurationNotable Features
DiazepamValiumLong-actingRapid onset; used for anxiety, seizures, muscle spasms, alcohol withdrawal; active metabolites prolong effects
LorazepamAtivanIntermediateNo active metabolites; safe in liver impairment; commonly used in acute agitation; IM administration well-absorbed
AlprazolamXanaxShort-actingMost commonly prescribed benzodiazepine; high abuse potential; significant rebound anxiety; commonly used for panic disorder
ClonazepamKlonopinLong-actingUsed for panic disorder, seizures, social anxiety; longer duration reduces interdose rebound
ChlordiazepoxideLibriumLong-actingHistorically used for alcohol withdrawal protocols; first benzodiazepine synthesized
TriazolamHalcionUltra-shortUsed as a hypnotic (sleep aid); risk of anterograde amnesia; very short half-life

Clinical Considerations

  • Rapid onset of action (minutes to hours), unlike antidepressants which take weeks
  • Tolerance and dependence develop with chronic use; benzodiazepines should generally be prescribed for short-term use
  • Withdrawal can be medically dangerous (seizures, delirium); must be tapered gradually, never stopped abruptly
  • Cross-tolerance exists with alcohol and barbiturates (all act on GABA receptors)
  • Benzodiazepines are respiratory depressants; combined with opioids or alcohol, the risk of fatal respiratory depression increases significantly
  • Older adults are at increased risk for falls, cognitive impairment, and paradoxical reactions (agitation, disinhibition)
Flumazenil (Romazicon)

Flumazenil is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose. It competitively blocks the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor. Caution: it can precipitate seizures in patients with benzodiazepine dependence.
prev_last_paragraph: This chapter covers anxiolytics (medications used to treat anxiety disorders), including benzodiazepines and buspirone, as well as anti-dementia medications. These medication classes appear regularly on the EPPP because understanding their mechanisms, side effects, and clinical considerations is essential for psychologists collaborating with prescribers.

section_html:
Buspirone (BuSpar)

Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic used primarily for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).

  • Mechanism: Partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors; does not act on GABA receptors
  • Onset: Takes 2-4 weeks to reach full effect (similar to antidepressants), making it unsuitable for acute anxiety relief
  • Advantages: No sedation, no tolerance or dependence, no withdrawal syndrome, no cross-tolerance with alcohol/benzodiazepines, no abuse potential
  • Disadvantages: Slow onset; not effective for acute anxiety or panic; patients who have previously used benzodiazepines may perceive it as ineffective due to the absence of the immediate sedating effect
EPPP Tip

Buspirone is a favorite EPPP topic because it differs from benzodiazepines in every key way: slow onset, no sedation, no dependence, no withdrawal, no cross-tolerance with alcohol. If a question asks about an anxiolytic that is safe for patients with a history of substance abuse, buspirone is the answer.
prev_last_paragraph: Flumazenil is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose. It competitively blocks the benzodiazepine binding site on the GABA-A receptor. Caution: it can precipitate seizures in patients with benzodiazepine dependence.

section_html:
Anti-Dementia Medications

Currently available medications for Alzheimer's disease provide symptomatic relief but do not halt or reverse the underlying neurodegenerative process.

Cholinesterase Inhibitors

These drugs inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down acetylcholine, thereby increasing acetylcholine availability in the brain. They are used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease.

Generic NameBrand NameNotable Features
DonepezilAriceptMost commonly prescribed; once-daily dosing; approved for all stages of Alzheimer's; relatively well-tolerated
RivastigmineExelonAvailable as a transdermal patch (reduces GI side effects); also inhibits butyrylcholinesterase; approved for Parkinson's disease dementia
GalantamineRazadyneAlso modulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

Common side effects: Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, decreased appetite, dizziness, bradycardia (all related to increased cholinergic activity).

Memantine (Namenda)

  • Mechanism: NMDA receptor antagonist; blocks excessive glutamate activity (thought to protect against excitotoxicity)
  • Uses: Moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease; often used in combination with a cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Side effects: Generally well-tolerated; dizziness, headache, constipation, confusion
EPPP Tip

Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) work by increasing acetylcholine and are used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's. Memantine is an NMDA antagonist used for moderate to severe Alzheimer's. These drugs slow symptom progression but do NOT cure or reverse the disease.
prev_last_paragraph: Clinical NoteA musician experiencing hand tremor and rapid heartbeat before recitals may benefit from a single dose of propranolol taken 30–60 minutes before performing. However, a patient with pervasive worry, rumination, and emotional distress associated with GAD would not find adequate relief from a beta-blocker alone, because these drugs do not target the psychological dimensions of anxiety.

section_html:
Standard 9.03: Informed Consent in Assessments

Psychologists obtain informed consent for assessments, evaluations, or diagnostic services, except when:

  1. Testing is mandated by law or governmental regulations
  2. Informed consent is implied because testing is conducted as a routine educational, institutional, or organizational activity (e.g., admission testing)
  3. The purpose of the testing is to evaluate decisional capacity

9.03(a) -- Explaining the Purpose

Informed consent includes an explanation of the nature and purpose of the assessment, fees, involvement of third parties, and limits of confidentiality in a language reasonably understandable to the person being assessed or their legal representative.

9.03(b) -- Individuals Lacking Capacity

For persons who lack the capacity to consent (e.g., due to cognitive impairment), psychologists provide appropriate explanation, seek the person's assent, consider preferences and best interests, and obtain consent from a legally authorized person.

9.03(c) -- Court-Ordered or Mandated Assessment

When services are court ordered or otherwise mandated, psychologists inform the individual of the nature of the anticipated services, including whether the services are court ordered or mandated and any limits of confidentiality, before proceeding.

EPPP Tip

Court-ordered assessments still require notification -- the psychologist must tell the individual about the nature of services and limits of confidentiality, even though the person cannot refuse the assessment. Informed consent is modified but not eliminated in mandated evaluations.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist administers an intelligence test normed on English-speaking Americans to a recent immigrant whose first language is Spanish. The psychologist must note the cultural and linguistic limitations of the assessment, consider using instruments validated for Spanish speakers, and avoid drawing definitive conclusions about intellectual ability based on the potentially biased results.

section_html:
Standard 9.05: Test Construction

Psychologists who develop tests and other assessment techniques use appropriate psychometric procedures and current scientific or professional knowledge for test design, standardization, validation, reduction or elimination of bias, and recommendations for use.

This standard applies to psychologists who create new assessment instruments and requires that such instruments meet accepted standards for reliability, validity, and fairness.
prev_last_paragraph: Test data (9.04) = the client's responses, scores, and behavioral observations -- generally released to the client upon request. Test materials (9.11) = the test itself (questions, stimuli, manuals, scoring keys) -- protected from release to maintain test security. A helpful mnemonic: test data are about the person; test materials are about the test. If a document would exist regardless of which client sat down — such as a test manual or a blank answer sheet — it is a test material. If it was created because this particular client participated — such as their scores, their specific answers, or your behavioral observations — it is test data. This distinction is frequently tested on the EPPP.

section_html:
Standard 2.01: Boundaries of Competence

This subsection establishes the fundamental rule: psychologists provide services, teach, and conduct research only within the boundaries of their competence.

2.01(a) -- Education, Training, and Experience

Psychologists provide services in areas in which they have established competence through education, training, supervised experience, consultation, study, or professional experience. Competence is typically demonstrated through:

  • Graduate coursework in the specific area
  • Supervised clinical or research experience
  • Postdoctoral training or specialty fellowships
  • Continuing education in the specific domain
  • Peer consultation and supervision

2.01(b) -- New Areas of Practice

When psychologists wish to provide services in areas where recognized professional standards do not yet exist, they take reasonable steps to ensure the competence of their work and to protect clients, students, and others from harm. This provision acknowledges that psychology is an evolving field.

Example

A psychologist trained in cognitive-behavioral therapy wants to begin providing telepsychology services. Under 2.01(b), the psychologist should obtain training in telehealth best practices, learn the relevant technology, understand the legal requirements of interstate practice, and seek consultation from colleagues experienced in telepsychology before beginning.

2.01(c) -- Unfamiliar Populations

In areas where recognized training standards for serving specific populations do not yet exist, psychologists with closely related prior training or experience may provide such services, with appropriate study, training, supervision, and/or consultation. This is particularly relevant to working with diverse cultural, ethnic, or linguistic groups.

2.01(d) -- Forensic Activities

When psychologists are asked to provide services to individuals for whom appropriate mental health services are not available and for which psychologists have not obtained the requisite competence, they may provide services with the closest related competence -- but only until a qualified provider becomes available.

2.01(e) -- New Techniques

In emerging areas where generally recognized standards for preparatory training do not yet exist, psychologists take reasonable steps to ensure competence and protect clients from harm.

2.01(f) -- Familiarity with Relevant Factors

When assuming forensic roles, psychologists must be knowledgeable about the judicial or administrative rules governing their participation.
prev_last_paragraph: Professional competence refers to the ability to effectively and appropriately apply the knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary to fulfill one's professional roles. It encompasses both intellectual understanding and practical skill, shaped by ongoing education and experience.

section_html:
Standard 2.03: Maintaining Competence

Psychologists undertake ongoing efforts to develop and maintain their competence. This includes:

  • Staying current with scientific and professional developments in their areas of practice
  • Pursuing continuing education (CE) activities
  • Engaging in peer consultation and supervision
  • Reviewing current literature and research findings
  • Attending professional conferences and workshops

Continuing Education Requirements

Most state licensing boards require psychologists to complete a specified number of continuing education (CE) credits during each renewal period (typically 20-40 hours per biennium). Many states require specific CE topics such as ethics, cultural diversity, or evidence-based practice.

The Competence Constellation Model

Rodolfa et al. (2005) proposed a competence constellation model that distinguishes between foundational competencies and functional competencies:

Foundational CompetenciesFunctional Competencies
Reflective practice and self-assessmentAssessment, diagnosis, and case conceptualization
Scientific knowledge and methodsIntervention
Relationships (therapeutic alliance)Consultation
Ethical and legal standardsResearch and evaluation
Individual and cultural diversitySupervision and teaching
Interdisciplinary systemsManagement and administration
prev_last_paragraph: Standard 2.02 is the emergency exception to competence boundaries. On the EPPP, if a question describes a crisis situation (e.g., a natural disaster) where no other provider is available, the psychologist may provide services outside their typical area of competence. However, this is temporary — they must stop once the emergency ends or a qualified provider is found. Watch for answer choices that frame this as an absolute rule ("a psychologist must never practice outside their competence"); the emergency exception makes such absolutes incorrect. Also note that both conditions must be present: there must be a genuine emergency, and other appropriate services must be unavailable. A psychologist cannot invoke this standard simply because a situation feels urgent if qualified providers are accessible.

heading_text: Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments
section_html:
Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments

Psychologists' work must be based on established scientific and professional knowledge of the discipline. This means psychologists should rely on:

  • Peer-reviewed research and empirical evidence
  • Established theories grounded in scientific investigation
  • Professional guidelines and practice parameters
  • Clinical judgment informed by training and experience, not personal bias or speculation
Evidence-Based Practice

The APA Presidential Task Force (2006) defined evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) as the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences. EBPP is the operational expression of Standard 2.04.

heading_text: Standard 2.05: Delegation of Work to Others
section_html:
Standard 2.05: Delegation of Work to Others

Psychologists who delegate work to employees, supervisees, research or teaching assistants, or others:

  • Take reasonable steps to avoid delegating work to persons with a multiple relationship with those being served
  • Authorize only those responsibilities the person can be expected to perform competently based on their education, training, or experience
  • Ensure that such persons perform the services competently
Example

A psychologist delegates psychological testing administration to a psychometrist. Under 2.05, the psychologist must ensure the psychometrist is properly trained in administering the specific test, must supervise the work appropriately, and retains ultimate responsibility for the interpretation and clinical use of test results.
prev_heading_text: Standard 2.04: Bases for Scientific and Professional Judgments
prev_last_paragraph: The APA Presidential Task Force (2006) defined evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) as the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences. EBPP is the operational expression of Standard 2.04.

section_html:
Standard 2.06: Personal Problems and Conflicts

This subsection addresses situations where a psychologist's personal problems may interfere with professional functioning.

2.06(a) -- Awareness of Personal Problems

Psychologists refrain from initiating an activity when they know or should know that there is a substantial likelihood that their personal problems will prevent them from performing their work-related activities in a competent manner.

2.06(b) -- Taking Appropriate Action

When psychologists become aware of personal problems that may interfere with their performing work-related duties adequately, they take appropriate measures such as:

  • Obtaining professional consultation or assistance
  • Determining whether they should limit, suspend, or terminate work-related duties
  • Seeking personal therapy
  • Taking a leave of absence if necessary
EPPP Tip

EPPP questions about impaired psychologists test whether you know that the ethical response involves the psychologist taking responsibility for their own impairment. The first step is self-awareness; the second is taking appropriate corrective action (consultation, therapy, limiting practice). Colleagues who become aware of an impaired psychologist should attempt informal resolution (Standard 1.04) by speaking to the psychologist directly.

prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist delegates psychological testing administration to a psychometrist. Under 2.05, the psychologist must ensure the psychometrist is properly trained in administering the specific test, must supervise the work appropriately, and retains ultimate responsibility for the interpretation and clinical use of test results.

heading_text: Overview of Standard 7: Education and Training
section_html:
Overview of Standard 7: Education and Training

Standard 7 (Education and Training) of the APA Ethics Code governs the ethical conduct of psychologists in academic and training settings. This standard addresses program design, accuracy in teaching, student disclosure requirements, mandatory therapy, performance evaluation, and prohibitions on sexual relationships with students and supervisees.

These provisions protect students and supervisees who are in inherently unequal power relationships with their educators and training supervisors.

Structure of the Ethics Code

The APA Ethics Code consists of four major components:

  1. Preamble -- States the purpose and scope of the Ethics Code. It establishes that psychologists commit to increasing knowledge, improving conditions, and helping the public develop informed judgments about behavior.
  2. General Principles (A through E) -- Aspirational goals that guide psychologists toward the highest ideals. They are not enforceable but provide a framework for ethical reasoning.
  3. Ethical Standards (1 through 10) -- Enforceable rules that set mandatory obligations. Violations can result in sanctions, license revocation, or expulsion from APA.
  4. Introduction and Applicability -- Clarifies how the Code applies, its relationship to law, and issues of jurisdiction.

The Preamble

The Preamble describes the mission of psychology and the purpose of the Ethics Code. It acknowledges that psychologists occupy roles as researchers, educators, diagnosticians, therapists, supervisors, consultants, administrators, social interventionists, and expert witnesses. The Preamble stresses that the Code applies to these roles only in the context of scientific, educational, or professional activities.

General Principles (Aspirational)

The five General Principles guide psychologists toward ethical ideals. For the EPPP, memorize each principle and know that they are aspirational, not enforceable.

PrincipleCore FocusKey Idea
A: Beneficence and NonmaleficenceDo good; do no harmPsychologists strive to benefit those with whom they work and guard against factors that might lead to misuse of influence. They manage personal, financial, social, organizational, or political factors that could lead to harm.
B: Fidelity and ResponsibilityTrust, professional responsibilityPsychologists establish relationships of trust, are aware of their responsibilities to society and the communities they serve, and consult with colleagues to prevent unethical conduct. They donate a portion of professional time for little or no compensation (pro bono).
C: IntegrityHonesty, truthfulnessPsychologists seek to promote accuracy, honesty, and truthfulness. They do not steal, cheat, or engage in fraud, subterfuge, or intentional misrepresentation of fact. They keep promises and avoid unwise or unclear commitments.
D: JusticeFairness, equal accessPsychologists recognize that fairness and justice entitle all persons to access the contributions of psychology and to equal quality in processes, procedures, and services. They exercise reasonable judgment and take precautions to ensure bias does not lead to unjust practices.
E: Respect for People's Rights and DignityAutonomy, privacy, diversityPsychologists respect the dignity and worth of all people and the rights of individuals to privacy, confidentiality, and self-determination. They are aware of cultural, individual, and role differences including those based on age, gender, race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, language, and socioeconomic status.
EPPP Tip

A common EPPP question format presents a scenario and asks which General Principle applies. Remember: Principle B (Fidelity and Responsibility) is the one that mentions pro bono work and concern for colleagues' ethical behavior. Principle D (Justice) specifically addresses fairness and bias.
prev_heading_text: Introduction to the APA Ethics Code
prev_last_paragraph: Aspirational principles (General Principles A-E) describe the highest ideals of the profession but are not enforceable. Enforceable standards (Standards 1-10) set minimum behavioral expectations and can be used as the basis for ethics complaints and disciplinary action.

section_html:
Ethical Standards Overview (Standards 1-10)

The ten Ethical Standards are the enforceable component of the Ethics Code. Each standard contains multiple subsections addressing specific behaviors and obligations.

StandardTitleKey Topics
1Resolving Ethical IssuesConflicts with law/organizations, informal resolution, reporting violations, cooperating with ethics committees, improper complaints, discrimination against complainants
2CompetenceBoundaries of competence, providing services in emergencies, maintaining competence, bases for scientific judgments, delegation, personal problems
3Human RelationsUnfair discrimination, sexual harassment, multiple relationships, conflicts of interest, third-party requests, exploitative relationships, informed consent
4Privacy and ConfidentialityMaintaining confidentiality, discussing limits, recording, minimizing intrusions, disclosures, consultations, use of confidential information
5Advertising and Other Public StatementsAvoidance of false statements, statements by others, descriptions of workshops, media presentations, testimonials, in-person solicitation
6Record Keeping and FeesDocumentation, maintenance/dissemination/disposal of records, withholding records for nonpayment, fees and financial arrangements, bartering, referral fees, accuracy in reports to payors
7Education and TrainingDesign of programs, descriptions of programs, accuracy in teaching, student disclosure requirements, mandatory individual/group therapy, assessing student performance, sexual relationships with students
8Research and PublicationIRB approval, informed consent, deception, debriefing, inducements, animal research, reporting results, plagiarism, publication credit, sharing data, reviewers
9AssessmentBases for assessments, use of assessments, informed consent, release of test data, test construction, interpreting results, assessment by unqualified persons, obsolete tests, test scoring, explaining results, maintaining test security
10TherapyInformed consent, therapy with couples/families, group therapy, therapy with those served by others, sexual intimacies, interruption/termination of therapy
prev_last_paragraph: A common EPPP question format presents a scenario and asks which General Principle applies. Remember: Principle B (Fidelity and Responsibility) is the one that mentions pro bono work and concern for colleagues' ethical behavior. Principle D (Justice) specifically addresses fairness and bias.

section_html:
Applicability and Enforcement

Several important points about the scope and enforcement of the Ethics Code frequently appear on the EPPP:

  • The Ethics Code applies to APA members and to psychologists licensed under state laws that adopt the Code, covering professional, scientific, and educational activities.
  • The Code does not apply to psychologists' purely private conduct that is not connected to their professional roles.
  • Lack of awareness or misunderstanding of an Ethical Standard is not a defense to a charge of unethical conduct.
  • The Ethics Code is not intended to be a basis of civil liability; whether a psychologist has violated the Ethics Code does not itself determine legal liability.
  • The modifiers "reasonably," "appropriate," and "potentially" in the Standards allow for professional judgment but require that the psychologist's actions be justifiable given the circumstances.
  • When the Ethics Code establishes a higher standard than the law, psychologists must meet the ethical standard. When the law establishes a higher standard, psychologists must comply with the law.
Example

A state law requires psychologists to report suspected child abuse. Even if a psychologist feels that reporting might damage the therapeutic relationship, the legal mandate overrides the ethical preference for maintaining confidentiality. Conversely, if the Ethics Code requires informed consent in a situation where local law is silent, the psychologist should still obtain informed consent.
prev_last_paragraph: Some ethicists (e.g., Meara, Schmidt, & Day, 1996) argue that ethical codes focused solely on rules are insufficient. A virtue ethics approach asks not just "what should I do?" but "what kind of person should I be?" The virtues of prudence, integrity, respectfulness, and benevolence complement the enforceable standards of the Ethics Code.

section_html:
Standard 3.01: Unfair Discrimination

Psychologists do not engage in unfair discrimination based on age, gender, gender identity, race, ethnicity, culture, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, socioeconomic status, or any basis proscribed by law. This applies to all professional activities.

EPPP Tip

Note the word "unfair" in this standard. Not all differential treatment constitutes discrimination. For example, using age-appropriate assessment instruments or adapting therapy techniques for clients with disabilities is appropriate differential treatment, not unfair discrimination.
prev_last_paragraph: The standard applies across all professional roles -- therapy, assessment, research, teaching, supervision, and consultation -- and emphasizes that the power differential inherent in psychologists' roles creates special obligations to protect those with whom they work.

section_html:
Standard 3.02: Sexual Harassment

Psychologists do not engage in sexual harassment, which consists of sexual solicitation, physical advances, or verbal or nonverbal conduct that is sexual in nature and that either:

  • Is unwelcome, offensive, or creates a hostile workplace or educational environment, and the psychologist knows or is told this, or
  • Is sufficiently severe or intense to be abusive to a reasonable person in the context

Sexual harassment can occur between any parties in a professional relationship: psychologist-client, supervisor-supervisee, professor-student, or between colleagues.
prev_last_paragraph: Note the word "unfair" in this standard. Not all differential treatment constitutes discrimination. For example, using age-appropriate assessment instruments or adapting therapy techniques for clients with disabilities is appropriate differential treatment, not unfair discrimination.

section_html:
Standard 3.04: Avoiding Harm

Psychologists take reasonable steps to avoid harming their clients, students, supervisees, research participants, organizational clients, and others with whom they work, and to minimize harm where it is foreseeable and unavoidable.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist in a rural community discovers that a new therapy client is the parent of a child on the psychologist's daughter's sports team. This creates a social-professional overlap. Because the psychologist is the only provider within 100 miles, referral may not be practical. The ethical response is to carefully manage the boundaries, document the decision-making process, and consult with a colleague about how to minimize potential conflicts. The psychologist might discuss with the client that they may encounter each other at games, agree on how to handle those interactions (e.g., polite but brief acknowledgment, no discussion of therapy content), and revisit the arrangement periodically to ensure it continues to serve the client's best interests.

section_html:
Standard 3.06: Conflict of Interest

Psychologists refrain from taking on a professional role when personal, scientific, professional, legal, financial, or other interests or relationships could reasonably be expected to:

  • Impair their objectivity, competence, or effectiveness, or
  • Expose the person or organization with whom the professional relationship exists to harm or exploitation
Example

A psychologist is hired by a company to conduct fitness-for-duty evaluations. The psychologist also owns stock in a competitor company. If the evaluation results could affect the stock value of the competitor, a conflict of interest exists. The psychologist should disclose the conflict or decline the engagement.
prev_last_paragraph: Psychologists take reasonable steps to avoid harming their clients, students, supervisees, research participants, organizational clients, and others with whom they work, and to minimize harm where it is foreseeable and unavoidable.

section_html:
Standard 3.07: Third-Party Requests for Services

When psychologists agree to provide services at the request of a third party, they clarify at the outset:

  • The nature of the relationship with each party
  • The role of the psychologist (e.g., therapist vs. evaluator)
  • The probable uses of the services provided or information obtained
  • Limits of confidentiality

This standard commonly applies in forensic, organizational, custody evaluation, and insurance-related contexts.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist is hired by a company to conduct fitness-for-duty evaluations. The psychologist also owns stock in a competitor company. If the evaluation results could affect the stock value of the competitor, a conflict of interest exists. The psychologist should disclose the conflict or decline the engagement.

section_html:
Standard 3.08: Exploitative Relationships

Psychologists do not exploit persons over whom they have supervisory, evaluative, or other authority, such as clients, students, supervisees, research participants, and employees. Exploitation can be financial, sexual, emotional, or otherwise take advantage of the power differential.
prev_last_paragraph: Although formal authorization is not required for consultation when identifying details are disguised, best practice often involves informing clients during the informed consent process that consultation with colleagues may occur as part of providing quality care. This proactive transparency builds trust and avoids potential misunderstandings. Additionally, psychologists should exercise caution in small communities or specialized settings where even de-identified case details might inadvertently reveal a client's identity due to the limited pool of individuals who match certain clinical profiles.

section_html:
Sexual Relationships: Standards 3.05 and 10.05-10.08

Sexual intimacies with clients and other protected parties receive special attention in the Ethics Code:

SituationStandardRule
Sexual intimacies with current therapy clients10.05Always prohibited
Sexual intimacies with relatives/significant others of current clients10.06Always prohibited
Therapy with former sexual partners10.07Always prohibited -- psychologists do not accept as therapy clients persons with whom they have engaged in sexual intimacies
Sexual intimacies with former therapy clients10.08Prohibited for at least two years after termination, and even after two years only in the most unusual circumstances with the burden on the psychologist to demonstrate no exploitation
Sexual relationships with current students/supervisees7.07Always prohibited
EPPP Tip

The two-year rule (10.08) is one of the most tested facts in the Ethics domain. Remember: the two-year clock starts at termination, not at the start of therapy. Even after two years, the burden falls on the psychologist to prove the relationship is not exploitative. Most ethics scholars advise that sexual relationships with former clients should always be avoided.
prev_last_paragraph: A psychologist in solo private practice creates a professional will designating a trusted colleague — a licensed clinical psychologist in the same community — as her professional executor. The document specifies that, in the event of the psychologist's sudden incapacity, the executor will secure all client files, contact active clients to arrange referrals, and ensure that records are maintained in compliance with state retention requirements. The psychologist provides the executor with a sealed envelope containing the location of electronic and paper records, passwords for the electronic health record system, and a current list of active clients.

section_html:
Informed Consent in Therapy (Standard 10.01)

Psychologists inform clients as early as possible in the therapeutic relationship about:

  • The nature and anticipated course of therapy
  • Fees, billing practices, and insurance involvement
  • The limits of confidentiality
  • The extent and limits of the therapist's involvement of third parties
  • The client's right to refuse or withdraw from treatment
  • Potential risks and benefits of treatment
  • Available alternatives to the proposed treatment

When the client is legally incapable of giving informed consent (e.g., a minor or an individual adjudicated incompetent), the psychologist provides an appropriate explanation, seeks the individual's assent, considers preferences and best interests, and obtains appropriate permission from a legally authorized person.
prev_last_paragraph: The two-year rule (10.08) is one of the most tested facts in the Ethics domain. Remember: the two-year clock starts at termination, not at the start of therapy. Even after two years, the burden falls on the psychologist to prove the relationship is not exploitative. Most ethics scholars advise that sexual relationships with former clients should always be avoided.

section_html:
Therapeutic Index

The therapeutic index (TI) is a critical concept for understanding medication safety. It quantifies the margin between a drug's effective dose and its toxic or lethal dose.

Narrow Therapeutic Index Drugs

Drugs with a narrow TI have a small margin between the therapeutic and toxic dose. These drugs require careful dosing, blood level monitoring, and vigilance for drug interactions.

DrugTherapeutic RangeMonitoring Notes
Lithium0.6-1.2 mEq/LToxicity at >1.5 mEq/L; affected by sodium intake, hydration, renal function, and NSAIDs; requires regular blood level monitoring and renal/thyroid function tests
Carbamazepine4-12 mcg/mLAutoinduction of its own metabolism (levels decrease over first few weeks); requires CBC monitoring due to rare aplastic anemia; potent CYP3A4 inducer
Valproate50-125 mcg/mLHepatotoxicity risk; teratogenic (neural tube defects); monitor liver function and platelet counts
Clozapine350-600 ng/mL (suggested)Risk of agranulocytosis requires mandatory ANC monitoring; also monitor for metabolic syndrome, myocarditis, seizures

Wide Therapeutic Index Drugs

Drugs with a wide TI have a large margin of safety. Routine blood level monitoring is generally not necessary.

  • SSRIs -- wide therapeutic index; difficult to cause lethal overdose with SSRIs alone. This is a major advantage over TCAs and MAOIs, particularly in patients with suicidal ideation.
  • Most benzodiazepines (when taken alone) -- wide TI, but significantly narrowed when combined with other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids).
EPPP Tip

The EPPP frequently tests the clinical monitoring requirements for narrow therapeutic index drugs, especially lithium. Know the therapeutic range, signs of toxicity, and factors that alter lithium levels (dehydration, NSAIDs, diuretics, sodium restriction). Lithium toxicity presents as coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and can progress to seizures, coma, and death.
prev_last_paragraph: Haloperidol is a high-potency antipsychotic (effective at low doses, e.g., 2-10 mg), while chlorpromazine is a low-potency antipsychotic (requires higher doses, e.g., 200-800 mg). However, at their respective optimal doses, both achieve similar efficacy in treating psychotic symptoms. The key difference lies in their side effect profiles: high-potency agents cause more EPS; low-potency agents cause more sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects. This means that when a clinician chooses between these medications, the decision is not about which one "works better" for psychosis — they are comparably efficacious — but rather about which side effect profile is more acceptable for the individual patient.

section_html:
Drug-Drug Interactions

Drug-drug interactions are a major clinical concern and a frequently tested EPPP topic. Interactions can be classified into two broad categories:

Pharmacokinetic Interactions

These interactions alter the ADME of one drug by another, changing the drug's plasma concentration:

  • CYP450 inhibition -- one drug inhibits the metabolism of another, causing the second drug to accumulate (increased levels, greater risk of toxicity). Example: fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor) dramatically increases clozapine levels (CYP1A2 substrate), potentially causing toxicity.
  • CYP450 induction -- one drug induces (increases the expression of) CYP450 enzymes, causing a second drug to be metabolized faster (decreased levels, reduced efficacy). Example: carbamazepine (CYP3A4 inducer) reduces the effectiveness of oral contraceptives (CYP3A4 substrate).
  • Protein binding displacement -- one highly protein-bound drug displaces another from plasma proteins, transiently increasing the free fraction of the displaced drug.
  • Altered renal excretion -- drugs that affect renal function or urinary pH can alter the excretion rate of other drugs. Example: thiazide diuretics reduce lithium clearance, increasing lithium levels and toxicity risk.

Pharmacodynamic Interactions

These interactions occur when drugs act on the same or related receptor systems, altering the overall pharmacological effect without changing drug concentrations:

  • Additive effects -- the combined effect equals the sum of each drug's individual effect (1 + 1 = 2). Example: combining two CNS depressants (e.g., a benzodiazepine and alcohol) produces additive sedation.
  • Synergistic effects -- the combined effect is greater than the sum of individual effects (1 + 1 = 3). Example: combining an SSRI with an MAOI can produce synergistic serotonergic effects, potentially causing life-threatening serotonin syndrome.
  • Antagonistic effects -- one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another (1 + 1 = 0.5). Example: a dopamine agonist used for Parkinson's disease may counteract the dopamine-blocking effects of an antipsychotic.
EPPP Tip

Key drug-drug interactions to know: (1) SSRI + MAOI = serotonin syndrome (requires 2-week washout, 5 weeks for fluoxetine); (2) lithium + NSAIDs or diuretics = lithium toxicity; (3) carbamazepine + oral contraceptives = contraceptive failure; (4) fluvoxamine + clozapine = clozapine toxicity; (5) benzodiazepines + alcohol/opioids = respiratory depression. Psychologists must understand these interactions even though they typically do not prescribe, because they assess patient presentation and coordinate with prescribers.
prev_last_paragraph: The EPPP frequently tests the clinical monitoring requirements for narrow therapeutic index drugs, especially lithium. Know the therapeutic range, signs of toxicity, and factors that alter lithium levels (dehydration, NSAIDs, diuretics, sodium restriction). Lithium toxicity presents as coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and can progress to seizures, coma, and death.

section_html:
Standard 4.01: Maintaining Confidentiality

Psychologists have a primary obligation to take reasonable precautions to protect confidential information obtained through or stored in any medium. This includes:

  • Information obtained in clinical practice, research, teaching, and consultation
  • Data stored electronically, on paper, or in any other format
  • Information shared orally in sessions, consultations, or supervisory contexts

The duty extends beyond active professional relationships. Psychologists must protect confidential information even after the professional relationship has ended and after the client has died (in most jurisdictions).
prev_heading_text: Overview of Standard 4: Privacy and Confidentiality
prev_last_paragraph: Privacy is the right of individuals to control access to information about themselves. Confidentiality is the ethical obligation of the psychologist not to disclose information obtained in a professional relationship. Privilege (or testimonial privilege) is a legal right that protects clients from having their confidential communications disclosed in legal proceedings without their consent. Privilege belongs to the client, not the psychologist.

heading_text: The Tarasoff Duty: Duty to Warn and Protect
section_html:
The Tarasoff Duty: Duty to Warn and Protect

The landmark case Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California established the legal foundation for the duty to protect third parties from client violence.

Tarasoff I (1974) -- Duty to Warn

The California Supreme Court initially ruled that therapists have a duty to warn identifiable potential victims when a client communicates a credible threat of violence.

Tarasoff II (1976) -- Duty to Protect

On rehearing, the court expanded the ruling to establish a broader duty to protect, which may be discharged through various means, not solely by warning the potential victim. Protective actions include:

  • Warning the intended victim directly
  • Notifying law enforcement
  • Hospitalizing the client (voluntary or involuntary)
  • Increasing the frequency of therapy sessions
  • Modifying the treatment plan to reduce risk
  • Other reasonable steps to protect the identified victim
Elements Required for Tarasoff Duty

Most jurisdictions require: (1) a special relationship exists between the therapist and the dangerous individual (i.e., a treatment relationship); (2) the client makes a credible, serious threat of physical violence; and (3) the threat is directed toward an identifiable potential victim.

Variations Across Jurisdictions

Not all states have adopted the Tarasoff ruling. Some states have enacted statutes that impose a duty to warn or protect, while others have rejected it entirely. On the EPPP, the general principle tested is awareness that such a duty exists and knowing the basic elements required to trigger it.

Example

A client tells their therapist, "I'm going to kill my ex-wife when she picks up the kids on Friday." This statement involves a serious threat, an identifiable victim, and an apparent timeline. The therapist has a duty to take protective action, which may include warning the ex-wife, contacting police, and potentially seeking involuntary hospitalization for the client.

prev_last_paragraph: A common EPPP trap: A subpoena alone does NOT require disclosure of confidential records. The psychologist should consult an attorney, notify the client, and may assert privilege on the client's behalf. Only a court order (signed by a judge) compels disclosure. Know this distinction well.

section_html:
Confidentiality in Group Therapy

In group therapy, the psychologist cannot guarantee that other group members will maintain confidentiality. The ethical obligation is to:

  • Discuss the importance of confidentiality with all group members at the outset
  • Establish group rules regarding confidentiality
  • Inform members that the psychologist cannot guarantee that other group members will not disclose information
  • Address breaches of confidentiality if they occur within the group
prev_last_paragraph: Working with minors presents unique confidentiality challenges because the legal right to consent (and access information) typically belongs to the parent or legal guardian, while the therapeutic relationship depends on the minor's trust.

section_html:
Mandated Reporting

Psychologists are mandated reporters in all 50 states for suspected child abuse and neglect. Key points:

  • Reporting is based on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. Psychologists do not need to conduct an investigation before reporting.
  • Most states extend mandated reporting to elder abuse and abuse of dependent adults.
  • Failure to report when mandated can result in criminal penalties, civil liability, and ethics violations.
  • Good-faith reports are typically protected by immunity statutes that shield reporters from liability even if the report proves unfounded.
  • Mandated reporting obligations override both confidentiality and privilege.
